tables.heading_path: Front matter > Foreword
tables.caption: Foreword
tables.content:
Globally, 357 million new cases of these four (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and trichomoniasis) curable STI’s are acquired annually mostly by people aged 15-49 years. Sexually transmitted infections (STI’s) remain a priority in HIV response. Some viral STI’s, like human papillomavirus (HPV), HSV2 and HIV, are still incurable and can be deadly, while some bacterial STI’s like chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and chancroid are curable if detected and treated.
A strong STI response will not only alleviate the burden of STI’s but will also have a beneficial impact on other health issues.. The STI response needs to be integrated with different health programmes and needs to be applied across sectors, including through school-based health education.
The Ministry of Health (MoH) as mandated by the Government of Eswatini prioritize STI’s, because of the correlation with other illnesses including HIV. STI’s play a major role in new HIV infections if not early diagnosed and managed properly. It is essential, therefore, that STI’s are properly managed at the first point of contact with health services.
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a significant threat to STI treatment, particularly for gonorrhea, classified by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a high-priority pathogen, and Mycoplasma genitalium, which exhibits resistance to first-line antibiotics. Multi-drug resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae has notably reduced treatment options. In response, the MfH is transitioning towards a bacteriology-driven approach, prioritizing testing where feasible to inform empiric treatment.
This strategy aims to improve treatment accuracy, minimize inappropriate antibiotic use, and mitigate AMR progression. While syndromic management will remain essential in resource-limited settings, laboratory confirmation will be promoted in well-resourced areas to ensure pathogen-specific treatment, strengthening STI control and supporting sustainable treatment.
This guideline for management of sexually transmitted infections in the Kingdom of Eswatini is building upon the vision of zero new infections, zero STI-related complications and deaths, and zero discrimination and it aims at ending the STI epidemic as a major public health concern. To address the limitation of etiological and presumptive diagnosis, the syndromic management approach to STI’s will be emphasized in the implementation of this guideline in all health facilities.
In line with the 2030 global targets, the guideline aims at 90% reduction of T. pallidum incidence; 90% reduction in N. gonorrhoeae incidence; ≤ 50 cases of congenital syphilis per 100 000 live births; Sustain 90% national coverage and at least 80% in every region in the country.
DR. V OKELLO
DIRECTOR OF HEALTH SERVICES.
MINISTRY OF HEALTH (MoH)

tables.heading_path: Front matter > Background
tables.caption: Background
tables.content:
STIs affect both men and women, and almost half of all STIs occur in people younger than 25 years old. Exposure to an STI can occur any time you have sexual contact with anyone that involves the genitals, the mouth (oral), or the rectum (anal). Exposure to STIs is more likely if you have more than one sex partner or do not use condoms. Some STIs can be transmitted through other routes, such as by sharing needles or needle pricks, during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding. Others may be asymptoms but still infectious.
STIs remain a priority in the HIV response. They constitute a major health and economic burden worldwide, and account for a substantial number of economic losses that are sustained in developing nations due to various morbidities. Globally, WHO estimates that more than one million curable STIs are acquired every day among people aged 15-49 years, amounting to 374 million new infections of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis in 2020. An estimated 8 million adults aged 15-49 years acquired syphilis in 2022, and approximately 520 million people in this age group are living with herpes simplex virus type 2 [15]. Prevalence of these infections is highest in the WHO African Region.
In Eswatini, the number of clients presenting with STIs at health facilities more than doubled between 2021 and 2024, rising from 11,129 to 25,351, and remained at a similar level of 25,221 in 2025. Women accounted for 62% of 2025 presentations and men 38%. The highest caseloads were recorded in Manzini (8,542; 33%) and Hhohho (6,478; 25%), followed by Lubombo (5,362; 21%) and Shiselweni (5,253; 21%). The burden is concentrated in young adults: adolescent girls and young women aged 15-24 years accounted for 5,483 presentations, women aged 25-34 years for 5,368, and men aged 15-34 years for 6,508 [16]. Eswatini also carries one of the world's highest adult HIV burdens, with adult HIV prevalence of 24.8% and incidence of 0.62% [17], and 6,701 new HIV diagnoses among 213,516 people tested in 2024 [18]. This overlapping epidemiology makes the STI consultation one of the highest-yield entry points for HIV prevention, testing and treatment [19].
The factors that determine healthy sexual behaviour are complex and context-specific. In Eswatini, behaviours that pose high risks for STI and HIV transmission include; Low levels of knowledge about STIs and HIV; Inconsistent condom use; Multiple sexual partners; Gender disparities leading to unequal power in sexual decision-making and Inappropriate health seeking behaviour for STIs. The 2025 national programme review [16,20] further identified inadequate syphilis and hepatitis B screening and treatment in antenatal care, and voluntary medical male circumcision coverage of 48% against a 70% target, as persisting service-delivery gaps in STI and viral hepatitis prevention.
Effective management is one of the cornerstones of STI control as it prevents the development of complications and sequel. It decreases the spread of these diseases in the community and offers a unique opportunity for targeted education about HIV prevention and other STI’s. Appropriate treatment of STI at the first contact between patient and health care provider is therefore an important public health measure.
The use of standardized national protocols is strongly recommended to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the health care delivery. All health facilities that provide STI services should implement the STI service package as outlined in this guideline. The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates a shift in STI management strategies, particularly for gonorrhea and Mycoplasma genitalium, which have shown resistance to commonly used antibiotics, limiting treatment options. The emergence of multi-drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a WHO-designated priority pathogen of public health concern, underscores the urgent need for bacteriology testing to identify resistance patterns and guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Laboratory confirmation nonetheless remains limited: fewer than 200 detections of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis combined were recorded nationally through molecular (GeneXpert) testing in 2025, concentrated in the 15-29 year age bands, against more than 25,000 clinical STI presentations in the same period [16]. These counts reflect the current reach of molecular testing rather than the true burden of infection, and the gap between clinical presentations and confirmed diagnoses underlines the need to expand testing coverage and strengthen STI laboratory reporting. While syndromic management remains fundamental, Eswatini’s approach now emphasizes specimen collection and bacteriology testing where feasible, ensuring pathogen-specific treatment to optimize antibiotic use, reduce treatment failures, and curb AMR development. The purpose of this guideline is to standardize and recommend harmonized provision of comprehensive, quality and client centered STI prevention and treatment services. The goal is to promote service uptake resulting in improved client outcomes and elimination of STI infection including related complications.

tables.heading_path: Front matter > Rationale for the STIs guidelines
tables.caption: Rationale for the STIs guidelines
tables.content:
There are several challenges to providing effective STI services to the people who need them. Many people with STIs do not seek treatment because they are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms and do not realize that anything is wrong. Others who have symptoms due to stigma associated with STI’s may prefer self-medication or seek treatment at pharmacies or from traditional healers. Even those who come to a clinic may not be properly adhere or complete treatment course. In the end, only a small proportion of people with an STI may be cured and avoid reinfection. This Guideline aims to help increase the proportion of STI patients that are treated and cured through assisting health care providers to:
- Raise awareness in the community about STIs and how they can be prevented - especially among populations who may be at high risk.
- Promote safer sexual practices, including delaying sexual onset, consistent condom use and having one or fewer partners.
- Promote early use of clinic services to cure STIs and prevent complications. Teach people how to recognize symptoms and when to seek care.
- Screening for asymptomatic infection for all sexually active clients.
- Manage symptomatic STIs effectively. Follow syndromic management guidelines for STI case management.
- Counsel patients on staying uninfected after treatment. Encourage them to comply with treatment, assist with partner notification and treatment, and reinforce prevention.
A combined strategy of effective community interventions and improved clinical services can have a large impact on STIs and their complications. Better clinical services increase the number of people who are cured. More effective prevention in the community, especially when it reaches those at highest risk, can reduce the overall STI problem. The combination of strategies benefits everyone.

tables.heading_path: Front matter > Target audience
tables.caption: Target audience
tables.content: These guidelines will be part of a consolidated set of guidelines for the prevention of STIs and management of people with STIs that are intended for programme managers for STI prevention and control at the national level and the health-care providers at the frontline in primary, secondary and tertiary health-care facilities. For the programme managers, the guidelines will assist in deciding how to organize the services for providing STI care and to determine the distribution of equipment and commodities that ensure access to high-quality STI care for people. The guidelines can also be used as an advocacy tool for the financial and human resources required to deliver adequate, acceptable and equitable STI care for everyone who needs STI services. Similarly, these guidelines can offer guidance to policy-makers other stakeholders and partners in providing services for STI prevention, treatment and care.

tables.heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases
tables.caption: 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases
tables.content:
Effective management is one of the cornerstones of STI control. It prevents the development of complications, sequela and decreases the spread of these diseases in the community. Offers a unique opportunity for targeted education about HIV prevention and other STI’s. Appropriate treatment of STI at the first contact between patient and health care provider is therefore an important public health measure.
The use of standardized national protocols is strongly recommended in order to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the health care system delivery. Standardized treatment facilitates training and supervision of health providers and, this in turn delays the development of antimicrobial resistance in STIs.
Etiological diagnosis: Ideally, the diagnosis of an STI is made by knowing exactly what organism is present by performing laboratory tests. Unfortunately, this method of e diagnosis is often expensive and requires sophisticated equipment and skilled personnel to carry out. This places constraints on time, resources, costs and access to treatment for the patients. In addition, test results may not be available during the consultation, thus requiring patients to return in one or two days. This is not feasible in many settings. The risk of developing complications is high and the period of infectivity is prolonged by this delay in therapy.
To enhance etiological diagnosis, sample collection should be integrated into routine STI care, where feasible. Specimen collection methods vary depending on the suspected STI and the site of infection. The following approaches can be used:
- Urine samples: Used for Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAATs) to detect Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in both males and females.
- Urethral or endocervical swabs: Collected for gram stain, culture, and NAATs, aiding in identifying gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Mycoplasma genitalium.
- Vaginal swabs: Self-collected or clinician-obtained samples can be used for bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and candidiasis testing.
- Blood samples: Used for serological tests (e.g., RPR or TPHA for syphilis, HSV IgG/ IgM for herpes, and HIV screening).
- Lesion or ulcer swabs: Collected for herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR testing, syphilis dark-field microscopy, or Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) culture.
- Rectal and pharyngeal swabs: Recommended for high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), to diagnose extragenital gonorrhea and chlamydia infections.
By incorporating sample collection into clinical workflows, healthcare providers can increase diagnostic accuracy, improve antibiotic stewardship, and contribute to AMR surveillance efforts.
NB: Please refer to the relevant Specimen Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for detailed guidelines.
Clinical diagnosis: This involves using clinical experience to match identified symptoms and signs to a specific STI. However, even experienced specialists often misdiagnose STIs when they rely only on clinical experience. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies found that a clinical (syndromic) diagnosis of genital ulcer disease detected only about half of syphilis cases (pooled sensitivity 52.8%) and fewer than half of herpes cases (43.5%), while being somewhat better for chancroid (71.9%); the authors concluded that relying on clinical diagnosis alone results in significant numbers of missed cases and that affordable point-of-care diagnostics are urgently needed (Loh et al., 2022) .

tables.content:
1. Chancroid: raised rough edges, beefy.

- Latent/late stage: gumma, and may affect the central nervous system.

tables.heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.3 Syndromic Approach:
tables.caption: 1.3 Syndromic Approach:
tables.content:
A syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms. The numerous and different STI pathogens produce a number of syndromes, hence a syndromic diagnosis is made when the patient’s signs and symptoms are matched to a particular STI syndrome. Syndromic approach offers treatment for more than one pathogen so that antimicrobial therapy is effective against all the pathogens that commonly cause the syndrome.
This approach to diagnosis and treatment reduces costs and increases access to treatment. This provides a more practical and cost-effective intervention for reaching the majority of patients with STI’s, especially in resource-limited settings. Syndromic STI management has some advantages which include the following:
Improved diagnosis
Advantages
- Can be administered by a wide range of primary health care workers (clinical officers, physician assistants, nurses, midwives)
- Allows treatment of a symptomatic patient in a single clinic visit
- Cheap, simple and cost-effective
- Permits treatment of mixed infections
- WHO still regards it as an essential component of STI control, and it remains the standard of care in resource-limited settings where lab diagnosis is unavailable or slow.
Challenges
- Overdiagnosis and overtreatment can increase drug costs
- Risk of multiple-drug side effects, drug interactions, altered vaginal flora, and antimicrobial resistance - WHO now treats overtreatment as increasingly undesirable given worsening resistance and limited treatment options.
- Not useful for detecting infections in asymptomatic individuals
- Vaginal discharge poorly predicts cervical gonococcal/chlamydial infection; WHO acknowledges its vaginal discharge flowcharts have limitations for cervical infections.
- Leaves a gap in establishing antimicrobial susceptibility for patients failing first-line therapy, especially gonococcal infections.
Key message: The Ministry of Health recommends that all patients presenting with STI’s are treated using the syndromic management approach, but when available, guided with quality-assured rapid tests, bacteriological and molecular assays for STI laboratory diagnosis

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components
tables.caption: 2.0 Essential Components
tables.content:
- History taking: Includes demographic information, a behavioural risk assessment, and medical history to identify potential exposures and risk factors.
- Physical examination: Focuses on the genital, anal, and oral areas, along with a skin assessment, to identify lesions, discharge, ulcers, or other STI-related signs.
- Establishing a syndromic and/or etiological diagnosis: Syndromic management remains a key approach in STI care, but etiological diagnosis is increasingly emphasised through laboratory testing. Where feasible, specimen collection (e.g. urethral, vaginal, cervical, or lesion swabs, urine samples, and blood tests) should be undertaken to confirm the causative pathogen, enable targeted treatment, and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, thereby helping to limit antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
- Curative therapy: Effective antimicrobials should be administered at the first point of contact to reduce transmission and complications. Given the rise in drug-resistant STIs, treatment regimens should be reviewed and updated periodically in line with local AMR surveillance data to maintain efficacy.
- Health promotion package: Education on STI prevention, condom use, partner notification, and risk-reduction strategies should be integrated into patient consultations. Patients should also be informed about AMR and the importance of completing the prescribed treatment course.
- Clinical follow-up and referral where necessary: Post-treatment review helps confirm treatment effectiveness and detect possible treatment failures. Patients with persistent or recurrent symptoms should undergo laboratory testing, including antimicrobial susceptibility testing where available, to guide alternative treatment and limit onward transmission of drug-resistant STIs.
By combining syndromic management with bacteriological and molecular testing and structured post-treatment follow-up, Eswatini aims to strengthen STI control, slow the development of AMR, and improve long-term patient outcomes.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.1 History Taking and Assessing STI and HIV Risk > Gathering Patient Information
tables.caption: Gathering Patient Information
tables.content:
Information gathering strategies:
- Explain that all information will be kept confidential
- Develop a rapport so the patient can feel relaxed and comfortable
- Explore the patient’s concerns by practicing active listening
- Use a dynamic discussion between you and your patient as a means of taking the history, which should include an assessment of the patients risk level
- Take note of nonverbal cues.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.1 History Taking and Assessing STI and HIV Risk > Patient information to be gathered
tables.caption: Patient information to be gathered
tables.content:
Collect the following information during your patient centered discussion:
1. Name
2. Age, Sex
3. Physical address
4. Marital status
5. Presenting symptoms
6. History of presenting symptoms:
   - Discharge: duration, consistency, odour, color and amount
   - Burning, urgency and/or frequency of micturition and colour of urine
   - Swelling and/or pain in the groin
   - Lesion: location (vaginal, anal and oral), pain, ulcer, blister, bruises, indurations, rash, cracking
   - Lower abdominal pain in women: painful vaginal intercourse (dyspareunia)
   - Rectal discharge or pain
   - Difficulties with urination or defecation
   - Itching and/or discomfort in the perineum, peri-anal, and pubic areas
   - Itchy /Non-itchy skin rashes or warty lesions
7. Medical and gynecological history:
   - Ask ll females if they have ever been screened for cervical cancer
   - HIV status and proof of status/ testing history
   - Any chronic illness e.g. diabetes mellitus, If HIV+ and whether or not on ART
   - Medication history
   - Any known allergi
8. Social history:
   - Substance use: Alcohol, tobacco, and recreational drug use — including type, frequency, quantity, and route of administration. Specifically screen for sexualised drug use (chemsex) and injecting drug use, both of which are associated with elevated STI, HIV, and hepatitis C risk. Use standardised screening tools in a routine, nonjudgmental manner.
   - Transactional sex: Whether the patient has exchanged sex for money, housing, drugs, or other needs, as this is a recognised STI risk factor, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.
   - Intimate partner violence and sexual violence: Screen for current or past trauma, sexual abuse, or violence, as STI consultations may be the patient's only opportunity to access support and referral.
   - Psychosocial context: Living arrangements, employment status, and social support, which may affect treatment adherence, partner notification, and follow-up attendance.
9. Taking sexual history:
A sexual history should be taken from all patients before examination and management of their sexual health concerns. The patient must be assured that the information they provide is held in strict confidence. The clinical environment should be welcoming, nonjudgmental, and trauma-informed, as some patients may have experienced abuse or violence. The service provider should conduct a behavioural risk assessment, including:
- Partners: Number and gender of current and recent sexual partners, whether partners are new or regular, and whether partners have other concurrent sexual partners or known STI/HIV status.
- Practices: Sexual exposure sites (oral, anal, vaginal), specific sexual practices, and whether the patient meets partners through apps or online platforms — as these inform anatomical site-specific specimen collection and testing.
- Protection from STIs: Condom use with regular and/or casual partners (frequency and consistency), awareness and use of PrEP, and vaccination status for HPV, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B.
- Past history of STIs: Previous STI diagnoses, treatments received, recurrent symptoms, and whether partners were also tested and treated.
- Pregnancy intention: Whether the patient or their partner intends pregnancy, current contraception use, and need for reproductive health counselling.
- Additional risk factors: Transactional sex (exchanging sex for money, housing, drugs, or other needs), sexualised drug use (chemsex), and intimate partner violence or sexual coercion - as these significantly elevate STI acquisition risk and may require referral to additional services
10.Past STI history:
- Have you ever been tested for STIs or HIV? When was your most recent test?
- Have you ever been diagnosed with an STI? If so, which infection(s) and when?
- Were you the index patient or were you identified as a contact through partner notification?
- If you were the index patient, was your partner(s) notified, tested, and treated?
- Did you complete the full course of treatment as prescribed?
- Did you return for a follow-up visit or test of cure after treatment?
- Have you had any symptoms that keep coming back, such as discharge, sores, or pain?
- Do you know the STI or HIV status of your current partner(s)?
A thorough sexual history will guide appropriate risk reduction and prevention counseling. There are several barriers to open and frank discussions of sexual health issues between patient and service provider.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2 Physical examination
tables.caption: 2.2 Physical examination
tables.content: Before examining a patient, obtain consent, explain each step in advance, and ensure privacy and comfort throughout the examination. Adhere to safety precautions like hand hygiene, glove use, and safe disposal of sharps. Conduct examinations in a well-lit room, exposing only the area needed while keeping the patient covered. Communicate findings using language the patient understands, and perform all procedures gently with minimum discomfort. Have consideration of the client's choice in the sex/gender of the attendant as per provisions in the Health Act of 2023.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2.1 Physical examination of the female
tables.caption: 2.2.1 Physical examination of the female
tables.content: Conduct a systematic general examination, inspecting the skin, palms, hair, lymph nodes (cervical, axillary, inguinal), and external genitalia for rashes, ulcers, warts, discharge, or swellings, documenting the size, location, and appearance of all lesions. For female patients, perform a speculum examination to inspect the vaginal walls and cervix for ulcers, warts, and discharge, and offer cervical cancer screening (Pap smear or VIA) if not performed within the recommended interval. Follow with a bimanual examination to assess for adnexal masses, tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. Note that speculum and bimanual examinations may need to be deferred if the patient has extensive, painful genital ulcers.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.2.2 Physical examination of the male
tables.caption: 2.2.2 Physical examination of the male
tables.content: Inspect the skin of the neck, chest, back, hands, palms, lower abdomen, inguinal areas, and thighs for rashes and sores, and palpate the cervical, axillary, supraclavicular, epitrochlear, and inguinal lymph nodes for enlargement or buboes. Inspect the pubic hair for lice or nits, and examine the penis, including the meatus with foreskin retraction, looking for ulcers, warts, discharge, or other abnormalities. If no discharge is visible, gently squeeze and massage the urethra forward to express any discharge. Palpate the scrotal contents and inguinal regions, and document the size, location, and appearance of all lesions found.

tables.heading_path: 2.0 Essential Components > 2.3. Laboratory testing
tables.caption: 2.3. Laboratory testing
tables.content: Laboratory testing is essential for confirming STI and VH diagnoses, detecting asymptomatic infections, and guiding treatment decisions. Tests include rapid diagnostic tests, molecular assays, bacteriological culture, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, performed based on availability at each tier of the health system. Specimen collection may involve blood, urine, or swab samples depending on the suspected infection and anatomical site.

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package
tables.caption: 3.0 Health Promotion Package
tables.content:
- Educate the patient on treatment adherence, promote correct and consistent condom and lubricant use, and counsel on abstinence during treatment.
- Offer HIV counselling and testing, PrEP, voluntary medical male circumcision, and cervical cancer screening as per national guidelines.
- Issue partner notification slips, emphasise the importance of partner treatment, and follow up on partner treatment status at review visits.

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3. 1 Health education and risk reduction counselling
tables.caption: 3. 1 Health education and risk reduction counselling
tables.content:
STI Education and Risk Reduction Counselling: An STI consultation is a unique opportunity to provide education and risk reduction counselling to patients most at risk. This should be an interactive process that builds on what the patient already knows. Providers should demonstrate respect, compassion, and a nonjudgmental attitude throughout.
Key counselling messages should cover:
- Diagnosis and treatment adherence: Explain the patient's diagnosis, its implications, and the prescribed treatment. Emphasise the importance of completing the full course of medication (the right drug, right dose, right route, right time) and explain how poor adherence contributes to antimicrobial resistance, making future infections harder to treat.
- Risk reduction and safer sex: Discuss methods for lowering STI and HIV acquisition risk, including abstinence, mutual faithfulness, and correct and consistent use of male or female condoms with lubricants . Explore any barriers the patient @perceives to practising safer sex and identify realistic behavioural changes they are willing to make .
- Partner notification and treatment: Stress the importance of ensuring all sexual partners are notified, tested, and fully treated to prevent reinfection and onward transmission.
- HIV and related services: Discuss the risk of HIV co-acquisition, offer HIV counselling and testing, and refer to additional prevention services (PrEP, voluntary medical male circumcision) as per national guidelines.
- Follow-up: Encourage prompt health-seeking behaviour for any recurrent symptoms, and reinforce that reinfection is possible if partners are not treated or risk behaviours continue.
- Before closing, confirm three commitments with the patient: to complete their treatment, to reduce risky sexual activities, and to ensure their sexual partners are fully treated.

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.2 Condom promotion and supply
tables.caption: 3.2 Condom promotion and supply
tables.content:
- The STI consultation is a key opportunity to promote, demonstrate, and distribute condoms, as patients are more likely to be receptive to understanding their role in preventing future STI/HIV exposure.
- Demonstrate correct condom use and support patients with partner negotiation skills to encourage consistent use.
- Provide condoms at the point of care, advise on where to access further supplies, and refer to the National Condom Distribution Guideline for additional guidance.

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.3 Notification and management of sexual partner(s)
tables.caption: 3.3 Notification and management of sexual partner(s)
tables.content:
Partner notification and treatment is one of the most important components of STI case management. It breaks the cycle of transmission, prevents complications, and identifies asymptomatic individuals who would not otherwise seek care. All partner notification must be conducted confidentially, voluntarily, and without coercion.
Partner treatment strategies:
- Offer immediate treatment to all sexual partners of the index patient, even if asymptomatic, using the same treatment regimen.
- Where a partner is unlikely to attend in person, consider providing the index patient with a prescription or medication for their partner (expedited partner therapy), particularly for populations with casual partners.
- Assess all partners for additional STIs beyond the presenting infection.
Approaches to partner notification:
- Patient referral (passive): The index patient takes responsibility for notifying and referring their partner(s) for treatment, either through direct conversation, accompanying them to a facility, or providing a contact/notification slip. Success depends on the quality of counselling the index patient receives and the provider's communication skills.
- Provider referral (active): A health care worker contacts the partner(s) directly. This may be necessary when patient referral is unlikely to succeed, but requires the index patient's informed consent to protect confidentiality.
- Providers should discuss both approaches with the patient and agree on the most appropriate method. In some cases, a combination of both may be used.

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.8 STI Reporting Systems
tables.caption: 3.8 STI Reporting Systems
tables.content: All health facilities (private and public) should record and report STI cases treated at their facilities using the approved National tools provided Health Management and Information System (HMIS).

tables.heading_path: 3.0 Health Promotion Package > 3.8 STI Reporting Systems > STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention interventions
tables.caption: STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention interventions
tables.content:
STI and Viral Hepatitis Prevention:
- Promote abstinence, delayed sexual debut, and mutual faithfulness as key prevention strategies.
- Ensure availability and correct use of male and female condoms for all sexually active individuals, particularly high-risk groups.
- Encourage periodic STI screening for sexually active individuals, especially those not using protection consistently.
- Provide education on STI and viral hepatitis prevention and risk reduction.
- Reinforce universal precautions when handling hazardous waste and infectious materials.
Priority populations for hepatitis B vaccination:
- Health care workers and frontline personnel (police, firefighters)
- Pregnant women (from second trimester until delivery)
- Newborns (birth dose) and children under five
- Key populations, including people who inject drugs
- HBV seronegative individuals receiving dialysis or kidney transplant
- Unvaccinated sexual abuse survivors

tables.heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH
tables.caption: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH
tables.content: Syndromic management remains the foundation of STI care in Eswatini, but WHO recommends that treatment be guided by quality-assured laboratory or point-of-care testing wherever such testing is available. Molecular tests - nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) - are the reference standard for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis and Mycoplasma genitalium, and may be performed either in a laboratory or at the point of care using platforms already deployed in the Eswatini network, such as GeneXpert. Culture retains a specific and irreplaceable role for N. gonorrhoeae: it remains the only method that yields an isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and is therefore essential to national AMR surveillance. Where no aetiological test is accessible, syndromic treatment should still be given at the first point of contact and the specimen referred onward where feasible. The tests set out in this section are drawn from the WHO manual Laboratory and point-of-care diagnostic testing for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV (fourth edition, 2023), the 2024 WHO updated recommendations for the treatment of N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis and T. pallidum and new recommendations on syphilis testing, and the 2025 WHO guidelines for the management of asymptomatic STIs.

tables.heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.2 Specimen collection and transport
tables.caption: 4.2 Specimen collection and transport
tables.content: Correct specimen collection determines the validity of every result that follows. Use only the swab and transport medium supplied with the test platform in use, label each specimen at the patient's side, and record the anatomical site sampled on the request form so that the laboratory can interpret the result correctly. Self-collected vaginal swabs perform as well as clinician-collected swabs for NAAT and should be offered where privacy allows. For extragenital infection, sample the site of exposure: a genital specimen will not detect pharyngeal or rectal infection. Where testing is not performed on site, transport specimens within the time and temperature range specified by the manufacturer and refer them to the nearest testing laboratory without delay.

tables.heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.3 Antimicrobial resistance surveillance
tables.caption: 4.3 Antimicrobial resistance surveillance
tables.content: N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and molecular tests cannot yet provide reliable susceptibility results from non-culture specimens. Sentinel facilities should therefore continue to collect urethral and endocervical specimens for culture and susceptibility testing, and results should be reported to the national AMR surveillance system so that first-line regimens in these guidelines can be reviewed against local data. Patients whose symptoms persist or recur after correctly completed treatment should be re-tested, and an isolate sought for susceptibility testing where possible, rather than being treated empirically a second time.

tables.heading_path: 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH > 4.4 Testing asymptomatic people
tables.caption: 4.4 Testing asymptomatic people
tables.content: Most STIs are asymptomatic, and syndromic management cannot reach them. WHO recommends targeted screening for gonorrhoea and chlamydia in high-prevalence settings where resources allow, prioritising pregnant women, sexually active adolescents and young people aged 10-24 years, sex workers, and men who have sex with r. Screening for sex workers and men who have sex with men should be offered at least annually, and six-monthly where feasible. Syphilis and HIV testing should be offered to every person attending for STI care, irrespective of symptoms, and to every pregnant woman at her first antenatal visit. Hepatitis B surface antigen testing should likewise be offered to all pregnant women to allow timely antiviral prophylaxis and birth-dose vaccination.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content:
Lower abdominal pain is one of the major signs of Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) which may be accompanied by cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination, a complaint of back pain, lower tenderness with or without guarding on abdominal examination.
All sexually active women presenting with a history of lower abdominal pain should be carefully evaluated for the presence of salphingitis and/or endometritis - elements of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). In addition, routine bimanual and abdominal examination should be carried out on all women with presumptive STI since some women with PID will not complain of lower abdominal pain. Hospitalization of patients with acute PID should be seriously considered when:
- The diagnosis is uncertain
- Surgical emergencies such as appendicitis and ectopic pregnancy cannot be excluded
- A pelvic abscess is suspected
- The patient is pregnant Risk factors: women with IUD have a higher risk of PID, particularly if the IUD had been inserted recently.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Etiology
tables.caption: Etiology
tables.content: N. gonorrhea, C. Trachomatis and bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis are most frequently responsible of this syndrome.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
Lower abdominal pain is a complex syndrome to identify. Several other important non-STI causes may produce similar symptoms and signs.
- In all suspected lower abdominal pain patients, bi-manual examination and speculum must be conducted.
- The physical examination should assess the general condition of the patient. In all cases, pregnancy-related conditions, as well as an acute abdominal tenderness, should be excluded.
- Elevated temperature, high pulse rate, bleeding and low blood pressure, for example, should alert to the possibility of severe pelvic infection.
NB: Such patients should be referred urgently.
- On palpation, if signs of peritonitis such as lower abdomen guarding and rebound tenderness or if abdominal masses are present, the patient must be referred accordingly for further management.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content:
M. genitalium causes symptomatic and asymptomatic urethritis among men and is the etiology of approximately 15%-20% of NGU, 20%-25% of nonchlamydial NGU, and 40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis.
Among women, M. genitalium has been associated with cervicitis, PID, preterm delivery, spontaneous abortion, and infertility, with an approximately twofold increase in the risk for these outcomes among women infected with M. genitalium, infections among women are also frequently asymptomatic.
Rectal infection with M. genitalium has been reported among 1%-26% of MSM and among 3% of women ( 941 ). Rectal infections often are asymptomatic, although higher prevalence of M. genitalium has been reported among men with rectal symptoms. Similarly, although asymptomatic M. genitalium has been detected in the pharynx.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Diagnostic Considerations
tables.caption: Diagnostic Considerations
tables.content: M. genitalium is an extremely slow-growing organism. Culture can take up to 6 months, and technical laboratory capacity is limited to research settings. NAAT for M. genitalium is FDA cleared for use with urine and urethral, penile meatal, endocervical, and vaginal swab samples . M. genitalium should be suspected in cases of persistent or recurrent urethritis or cervicitis and considered for PID.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Treatment
tables.caption: Treatment
tables.content: M. genitalium lacks a cell wall, and thus antibiotics targeting cell-wall biosynthesis (e.g., ß-lactams including penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective against this organism. Because of the high rates of macrolide resistance with treatment failures and efficient selection of additional resistance, a 1-g dose of azithromycin should not be used.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content: Inguinal and femoral buboes are localized enlargements of the lymph nodes in the groin area, which are painful and may be fluctuant (soft with a feeling of liquid inside). Inguinal bubo is rarely the sole manifestation of an STI and is usually found together with other genital ulcer disease. Buboes are usually caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) and Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1- L3. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is an non ulcerative sexually transmitted disease of the genital area caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. It is important to elicit history of recent genital ulcer and examine the external genitalia in all patients presenting with bubos so that effective management can be given.

tables.heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Etiology

tables.content: Neonatal conjunctivitis is the condition where the baby develops purulent conjunctivitis in one or both eyes within four weeks of birth. STI-related infections are passed from the mother to the neonate during vaginal delivery.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases
tables.caption: 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases
tables.content: In any health facility, there are instances when a client’s blood sample is tested for syphilis either as a routine practice such as screening of pregnant women or screening for syphilis in most-at-risk groups (for example, sex workers or new detainees in prison) or vulnerable populations (for example, victims of sexual abuse). Often, syphilis tests are done to rule out clinical suspicion of secondary syphilis in patients presenting with generalized skin rashes or lymphadenopathy, or to rule out latent syphilis in asymptomatic patients.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases > Serological tests for syphilis
tables.caption: Serological tests for syphilis
tables.content: There are two main types of serological (blood) tests for syphilis: non-treponemal tests (non-specific) and treponemal tests (specific).

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases > Non-treponemal tests
tables.caption: Non-treponemal tests
tables.content:
The Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) and the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) tests detect the antibody to cardiolipin, a component of normal mammalian cell membrane. Therefore, these tests are sensitive but not specific for syphilis.
The advantage of these tests is that the results can be quantified and used for monitoring the treatment over time. Usually, these tests are positive 4-5 weeks after the occurrence of infection. A titre of 1:8 and above indicates probable active disease or recent infection (treated or untreated), although the RPR/VDRL can be negative in up to 30% of primary GUS cases.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases > Treponemal tests
tables.caption: Treponemal tests
tables.content: Treponemal rapid diagnostic test (RDT/Tp), Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody test (FTA), the Treponema pallidum Haemagglutination Assay (TPHA) and the Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) assay are specific tests which, if positive, indicate true infection. Once they are positive, they remain positive for life even after successful treatment. Therefore, they cannot be used for monitoring the patient’s response to treatment.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases > Management
tables.caption: Management
tables.content: A patient who currently has no symptoms or clinical signs of syphilis but who tested positive on serological syphilis test is diagnosed as having latent syphilis. Cases of latent syphilis are further divided into early latent syphilis and late latent syphilis, depending on the duration of the illness. Treatment duration also differs accordingly. In situations where doubt exists regarding the correct classification of the stage of latent syphilis, overtreatment is warranted to avoid development of complications.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.1 Management of reactive syphilis test cases > Treatment regimens for reactive syphilis test cases
tables.caption: Treatment regimens for reactive syphilis test cases
tables.content:
Benzethine Penicillin, 2.4millionIU IM weekly, after testing for sensitivity, for 3 weeks. Alternative regimens for penicillin hyper- sensitive patients:
- Doxycycline, 100mg orally BID for 30 days (non-pregnant women).
- Erythromycin, 500mg orally QDS for 30 days (pregnant women).
Note that Jarish Herxheimer reaction (mild fever, body aches and initiation of symptoms within 2 to 12 hours of injection) can occur with penicillin injection. This should be treated with Paracetamol, 500 mg to 1 g orally QDS on 1st day. The patient should be warned of the possibility of a reaction.
source_flags: Reactive syphilis tests are treated with benzathine penicillin weekly for 3 weeks 'after testing for sensitivity' for everyone; a single dose is the treatment for early syphilis (Table 3), and routine penicillin skin testing is not recommended (see Annex 5 flag).

- Non-reactive → Clinical suspicion? (ulcer or rash present) → Yes → Treat presumptively; repeat RPR in 2-4 wks → Monitor with RPR/VDRL at 3, 6, and 12 months.
→ Fourfold decline in titre = adequate treatment response.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.2 Balanitis and balanoposthitis > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content: Balanitis refers to the inflammation of the glans penis, whereas balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans, foreskin and/ or shaft. The main complication of balanitis is phimosis, in which case the foreskin adheres to the inflamed and swollen glans penis and cannot be retracted.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.2 Balanitis and balanoposthitis > Etiology
tables.caption: Etiology
tables.content: Candida albicans or lactobacilli
source_flags: Balanitis etiology lists only 'Candida albicans or lactobacilli'; lactobacilli are normal flora, not a cause of balanitis (anaerobes, streptococci and T. vaginalis are usual non-candidal causes).

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.2 Balanitis and balanoposthitis > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
- The common presentation is that of itch and swelling of the glans and foreskin. Sometimes pain may be reported.
- Patient may have a history of recent high-risk sexual practice, such as unprotected sex.
- A history of vaginal discharge from the partner may also be reported.
The physical examination may reveal signs of inflammation (such as red colour of skin (erythema), oedema, heat and tenderness).
The texture of the skin will also be altered, with white patches or streaks in typical cases of candidal infection. Presence of genital ulcerations and urethral discharge should be sought, and if present should be treated according to the appropriate syndromic algorithms.
Secondary bacterial infection may occur, causing superficial ulcers or erosions. Service providers should be aware that balanitis/balanoposthitis is commonly associated with diabetes mellitus and therefore should be ruled out by doing a urinalysis for glycosuria in chronic or recurrent cases.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.2 Balanitis and balanoposthitis > Management
tables.caption: Management
tables.content:
Partners should be examined for the presence of vaginal discharge. Routinely offer male circumcision to uncircumcised male patients as part of the health promotion
package. If the condition is so severe that the foreskin cannot be retracted (phimosis such cases should be referred appropriately (for surgical intervention).

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.2 Balanitis and balanoposthitis > Recommended treatment regimens
tables.caption: Recommended treatment regimens
tables.content:
The treatment of balanitis or balanoposthitis consists of:
- Maintaining local hygiene by retracting the foreskin, if possible, when washing.
- Instruct patient to wash the affected area daily with weak saline solution (one teaspoon of salt dissolved in one litre of lukewarm water) and avoid soap while inflammatory. PLUS
- Application of an antifungal cream i.e Clotrimazole cream applied locally twice a day x 7
- Cloxacillin 500mg QID for 7 days and Metronidazole TDS for 7 days may be given if secondary bacterial infections present.
Patients with recurrent or severe balanitis or balanoposthitis should be screened for the presence of diabetes mellitus. If the test is positive, the patient should be referred for further management.

tables.caption: Figure 10 (picture): Assessment and management of a buccal problem in an STI context (printed caption: 'Flowchart for syndromic treatment of balanitis and balanoposthitis')
tables.content:
Assessment and management of a buccal problem in an STI context. Always offer HIV test!
- Small lesions ulcerated (or vesicular), grouped in clusters, painful? yes → Herpes possible: clean the area with mouthwashes; give paracetamol. Antiviral treatment: Acyclovir PO 400mg x3/day, for 5 or 7 days. This treatment reduces the duration of symptoms only if initiated within 5 days of a 1st episode (duration 7 days) or within 24 hours of a recurrence (duration 5 days).
- Presence of mouth ulcer(s), unique or multiple? yes → Mouth ulceration. Treat: Syphilis*: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM 2.4 MUI (half dose in each buttock) single dose (SD). If it is painful or/and regional lymph nodes or/and not resolving with first treatment - suspect soft chancre: add Azithromycin PO 1g SD. Recommend: treatment of partners from the last 3 months with the same treatment (benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM 2.4 MUI SD for syphilis and/or azithromycin PO 1g SD for soft chancre). Give azithromycin PO 1g SD to everyone. Abstain from sexual practices with contact with the ulcer or use condoms until the ulcer resolves. Follow-up consultation after 7 days.
- Presence of painless growths: wart(s) or condyloma? yes → Complicated warts: indication for surgical treatment, or with imiquimod. Refer to the hospital.
- Presence of a whitish coating in the mouth? yes → Pain on swallowing and/or dysphagia and/or extensive lesions on the pharynx?
   - yes → Oropharyngeal candidiasis: treatment fluconazole 400 mg/day, for 14 days. HIV-AIDS must be ruled out.
   - no → Oral candidiasis: treatment miconazole muco-adhesive, 1 tablet/day, for 7 days; if severe or recurrent: fluconazole PO 200 mg/day, for 10 days. HIV-AIDS must be ruled out.
- Presence of inflammation of the throat (in a context of fellatio)? yes → Pharyngitis: can be caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae; however, the big majority of pharyngitis are viral. If risk factors of STI** AND oral sex → NG/CT pharyngeal swab for PCR and syphilis RDT.

* The presence of the ulcers indicates an infection called 'early'. In this context, the treponemal test (SD Bioline, etc.) can still be negative in 30% of cases.
** FDR of STI, MSM, urethral discharge in the partner, context of sexual violence or prostitution, new partner or more than one partner in the preceding 3 months.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.3 Genital Warts > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content: Warts may not cause symptoms and can regress naturally. Also refered to as condyloma accuminata may be found in the genital, oral and anal areas. Herpes Papiloma Virus (HPV) is the causative organism for warts and may manifest as a single or a clusters of lesions. They may appear as soft pink cauliflower like growth in moist areas rarely syphilitic warts can present as flat or papillary in shape.
source_flags: The genital warts description calls HPV 'Herpes Papiloma Virus' (human papillomavirus) and lists syphilis among the causes of warts (condylomata lata are a different lesion).

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.3 Genital Warts > Etiology
tables.caption: Etiology
tables.content: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV type 6 and 11) Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) High risk types such as HPV-16 and HPV-18 are implicated in most cervical and other anogenital cancers.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.3 Genital Warts > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
Most infections do not have clinical symptoms HPV warts may appear as raised or soft pink cauliflower like growth in moist areas usually painless but may itch.
There are three varieties of exophytic warts, which are sexually transmitted:
1. Condylomata Acuminata : Moist or partially keratinized surfaces (e.g. introitus, anus, under foreskin). Typically, cauliflower appearance. HPV
2. Keratotic warts: finger-like projection, often cauliflower-like appearance and typically on dry skin (e.g. penile shaft, scrotum, labia majora).
3. Papular warts: Smooth surfaces, less finger-like projections than keratotic warts.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.4 Molluscum Contagiosum > Description
tables.caption: Description
tables.content: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a type of Pox virus. Transmission occurs most commonly through sexual or non-sexual contact, and is enhanced by friction or micro-trauma.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.4 Molluscum Contagiosum > Etiology
tables.caption: Etiology
tables.content: Poxy virus

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.4 Molluscum Contagiosum > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
- The typical eruption appears as a pearly white dome-shaped papule with central umblication from which caseous material can be expressed.
- These lesions mostly appear at the point of contact (such as the genital area).
- Individual lesions usually regress without treatment in 9-12 months.
- Generalized lesions, especially multiple lesions on face, may indicate immuno-suppression due to underlying infection.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.4 Molluscum Contagiosum > Management
tables.caption: Management
tables.content:
- Excision curettage: Each lesion should be thoroughly opened with a fine sterile needle.
- The contents should be expressed and the inner wall touched with either Phenol/ Silver Nitrate. OR Trichloroacetic acid 30% solution or Iodine solution.
- OR Apply Podophyllotoxin 0.5% to the individual lesion BID for 3days.
- OR Imiquimod 5% cream.
- OR Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.4 Molluscum Contagiosum > Cases for referral
tables.caption: Cases for referral
tables.content: Patients with generalized lesions should be encouraged to undergo HIV testing and counselling, if their sero-status is unknown. These patients should be referred to the dermatology unit for further management.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.5 Management of Survivors Of Sexual Violence > Definition
tables.caption: Definition
tables.content: Sexual violence is defined as “any sexual act, attempt to obtain a sexual act, unwanted sexual comments or advances, or acts to traffic women’s sexuality, using coercion, threats of harm or physical force, by any person regardless of relationship to the victim, in any setting, including but not limited to home and work”.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.5 Management of Survivors Of Sexual Violence > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
Survivors of sexual assault have experienced a traumatic event and should be rapidly evaluated to determine whether they need emergency medical, psychological or social intervention. It is important to remember that the trauma of the event may make examination difficult. Explain carefully the steps that will be taken and obtain written informed consent from the patient before proceeding with examination, treatment, notification or referral.
Key points
§Sexual violence is common but is frequently not talked about by the person concerned— health care workers should maintain a high index of suspicion. They should ask about experience of sexual violence or abuse. §Individuals who have been sexually abused may need shelter and legal protection. Psychosocial management includes counseling and supportive services , which should be available on-site or by referral. §Medical management includes prevention of pregnancy and infection, in addition to care of injuries. STI and HIV Post Exposure Prophylaxis and emergency contraception should be available. § Forensic examination should be available and document evidence for legal action.
§ Referral should be available if services cannot be provided on-site.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Preventing STI’s in victims of sexual abuse
tables.caption: Preventing STI’s in victims of sexual abuse
tables.content:
STI’s in victims of sexual abuse requires a detailed history of abuse or assault and complete examination of the victim and (if possible) the alleged offender. There is a high risk of STI’s in victims of sexual abuse when:
The alleged offender is known to have an STI or to be at high risk for STI’s; and/or Symptoms and signs of an STI are detected in history and physical examination. The scheduling of examinations should be based on the history of assault or abuse. The following recommendation for scheduling examinations should serve as a general guide, the incident is recent, and a follow-up visit (approximately one week after the last sexual exposure) is needed to repeat the physical examination and to collect additional specimens, in order to allow sufficient time for infections to incubate.
Similarly, to allow sufficient time for antibodies to develop, an additional follow-up visit at approximately 12 weeks after the last sexual exposure is also necessary to collect blood for RPR or RDT-Tp test and HIV testing (after pre-test counselling with consent). A single examination may be sufficient if the person has been abused overan extended period of time, and/or the last alleged episode of abuse has occurred. STI prophylaxis or presumptive treatment for person who has been sexually assaulted or abused is described in the table below:

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.5 Management of Survivors Of Sexual Violence > 7.5.1 Chart 11 (Figure 11)
tables.caption: Figure 11: Syndromic treatment for management of survivors of sexual violence
tables.content:
Suspected sexual violence → Take history and examine: HVS, microscopy, pregnancy test, HIV rapid test, hepatitis B status, syphilis RDT.

Presenting within 72 hours:
- Presumptive STI treatment [updated per WHO 2021]: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally stat PLUS metronidazole 2 g orally stat.
- HIV post-exposure prophylaxis [updated per WHO 2024]: initiate as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours; preferred 3-drug regimen TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + DTG; full 28-day course prescribed at first visit; provide starter pack if full course not available, with rapid follow-up; if HIV positive: refer for chronic HIV care.
- Hepatitis B [added]: initiate hepatitis B vaccination if unvaccinated; complete vaccination series at follow-up.
- Emergency contraception [updated window]: if pregnancy test is negative: levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally stat (up to 72 hours), OR ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally stat (up to 120 hours), OR copper IUD insertion (up to 120 hours, most effective method). If pregnancy test positive, refer to ANC. If negative, repeat test at 6 weeks.

Presenting after 72 hours:
- Presumptive STI treatment [updated per WHO 2021]: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally stat PLUS metronidazole 2 g orally stat.
- HIV status: HIV PEP is not recommended beyond 72 hours; if HIV negative: follow up per national guidelines; if HIV positive: refer for chronic HIV care.
- Hepatitis B [added]: initiate hepatitis B vaccination if unvaccinated; complete vaccination series at follow-up.
- Pregnancy status: if within 120 hours: emergency contraception still possible (ulipristal acetate or copper IUD); if pregnancy confirmed: refer to ANC and follow up; if no pregnancy: repeat test at 6 weeks.

Follow-up schedule [added]: 2 weeks: assess PEP adherence and side effects, wound review. 6 weeks: repeat pregnancy test, repeat HIV test, syphilis serology. 3 months: repeat HIV test, repeat syphilis serology. 6 months: final HIV test, complete hepatitis B vaccination series.

All survivors at every visit: advise on legal protection and support with medico-legal documentation; provide psychological first aid at time of crisis and ongoing mental health support (screen for PTSD, depression, anxiety); treat all physical injuries, including tetanus prophylaxis per wound status and immunisation history; if pregnancy resulted from the assault, therapeutic termination may be considered after consultation with relevant authorities per national law.

Sources (printed): WHO Guidelines for HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (2024); WHO Guidelines for the Management of Symptomatic STIs (2021); WHO Clinical Management of Rape and Intimate Partner Violence Survivors; CDC nPEP Guidelines (2025). Verify all regimens against Eswatini national formulary and guidelines before implementation.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.6 Genital Scabies > Definition
tables.caption: Definition
tables.content: Genital scabies is caused by the Scabies mite (Sarcoptes scabiei), and is transmitted by close contact with an infected case, either sexual or non-sexual.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.6 Genital Scabies > Etiology
tables.caption: Etiology
tables.content: Sarcoptes scabiei

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.6 Genital Scabies > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content:
- The main complaint with genital scabies is itching especially at night-time.
- On physical examination, erythematous papules can be seen mainly on the flexure surfaces of the body, such as the axillae, elbow, and wrist, inter-digital spaces, around the umbilicus, inner thighs and back of the knee.
- Finding burrows tunneled by the female mites in the inter-digital spaces is diagnostic of scabies infection.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.6 Genital Scabies > Management
tables.caption: Management
tables.content:
Recommended treatment regimens in adults
- Benzyl Benzoate (BB) 25% lotion, to be applied all over the body below the neck, after a bath, for two consecutive nights. Patient should bathe 24 hours after the second application, and have a change of clothing. Bed linen is to be washed properly and dried under sunlight. A second course of drug application may be given after 7~10 days, if required. OR
- Gamma Benzene Hex chloride (GBH) 1% lotion or cream applied as a very thin film all over the body below the neck at night without taking a bath, to be washed off thoroughly next day morning, after 8~10 hours. The application of the drug should be repeated after 7days, if required. Clothes should be washed properly and dried under sunlight. OR
- Permethrin 5% cream to be applied all over the body as a thin film and washed off after 8~10 hours. A second application is sometimes required. OR
- Sulphur 6% in petrolatum applied to the entire body from the back down for 3 nights after a bath. Patients may bath before re-applying the drug and should bath 24 hours after the final application. OR
- Crotamiton 10% cream to be applied to the entire body from the neck down at night for 2~5 nights and washed off thoroughly by taking a bath 24 hours after the last application.
Treatment in infants, children younger than 10 years, pregnant or lactating women Gamma Benzene Hexachloride is contra-indicated in pregnant women, lactating mothers, infants and patients of scabies with secondary infection or with eczematisation, as it increases the risk of absorption, leading to systemic toxicity, resulting in seizures and aplastic anaemia. It should be applied with caution in the elderly. It should not be applied near the eyes.
The recommended regimen is:
- Crotamiton 10% cream/ sulphur 6% in petrolatum/ Permethrin 5%cream to be applied as above.

tables.caption: Description:
tables.content: Pediculosis pubis or pubic lice infestation is caused by the pubic louse (Phthirus pubis). It can be transmitted during sexual contact.

tables.caption: Etiology

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.7 Pediculosis pubis > Clinical features:
tables.caption: Clinical features:
tables.content:
- The symptoms and clinical signs of the infection include severe itching around the pubic area, often resulting in scratching.
