tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.8 Human papilloma virus infection > Definition
tables.caption: Definition
tables.content: Cervical cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer death in developing countries worldwide. The primary underlying cause is infection with one of more high-risk types of the human papilloma (HPV) virus, a sexually transmitted virus. HPV type 16 and 18 has been associated with 70% of all cervical cancers reported. The virus has also been implicated in other genital cancers: the attribute risk for 40% of penile cancer, 42% of anal cancer in men and 46% of vulvae and vaginal cancer is HPV type 16 and 18 infection. Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 are rarely associated with cancer, but commonly cause ano-genital warts.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.8 Human papilloma virus infection > Pre-disposing factors
tables.caption: Pre-disposing factors
tables.content:
The key determinants of HPV infection for both men and women are sexual behaviors, including young age at sexual debut, high number of sexual partner(s), and having a partner who has multiple partners.
Smoking is a potential risk factor for cervical cancer. Most HPV infections (low- or high-risk) resolve spontaneously. However, high-risk HPV infections that persist may lead to the development of precancerous and invasive cancer. It usually takes 10-20 years for precursor lesions caused by HPV to develop into invasive cancers.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.8 Human papilloma virus infection > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content: Some types of HPV are warts, especially genital warts. Genital warts may appear as a small bump, cluster of lesions or sterm-like protrusions. They commonly affect the vulva, cervix, penis and scrotum. They may also appear around the anus and in the groin. They can range in size and appearance and be flat, small, large, or cauliflower shaped and may be white or flesh tone.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.8 Human papilloma virus infection > Preventive measures
tables.caption: Preventive measures
tables.content:
Effective prevention interventions against ano-genital cancer include screening for and treatment of pre-cancer and invasive cancer. All women and men presenting at health facilities should be offered a complete ano-genital examination to determine whether they have this HPV-related cancer.
It is recommended that all sexually active women should have regular cervical cancer screening in accordance with the national guidelines. Male circumcision should be offered to all uncircumcised male patients and partners. Smoking cessation interventions should be implemented at the individual and community levels. Highly effective vaccines against high-risk types of HPV have recently become available.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection
tables.caption: Hepatitis B and C viral infection
tables.content:
Chronic viral hepatitis is a persistent liver infection, most often caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV), leading to ongoing inflammation and liver damage lasting longer than six months. Transmission occurs through exposure to infectious blood or body fluids, including unprotected sex, sharing of needles or unsterilised piercing/cutting instruments, blood transfusion, and from mother to child around the time of birth. HBV is 50-100 times more infectious than HIV. Both infections can be entirely asymptomatic, present as an acute illness (nausea, fatigue, dark urine, jaundice), or persist as a chronic infection that, over years, can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer; HCV is now a curable infection. In 2016 WHO adopted a global strategy to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, targeting a 90% reduction in new infections, a 65% reduction in
mortality, and treatment of 80% of those eligible. Eswatini is a high HBV-prevalence country, estimated at 8.7% in the general population; HCV prevalence is lower, estimated at 0.4%. Globally, only around 13% of people living with chronic HBV have been diagnosed and about 3% are on treatment, underlining the importance of the screening and linkage-to-care steps below.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Clinical features
tables.caption: Clinical features
tables.content: Many people have no symptoms during the initial infection with either HBV or HCV. Some develop an acute illness with vomiting, jaundice, fatigue, dark urine and abdominal pain that resolves over a few weeks; rarely, fulminant hepatic failure and death can occur. Following primary HBV infection in adults, 6-10% of infected persons become chronic carriers, of whom about 25% develop chronic active hepatitis; 15-30% of chronic hepatitis cases progress to cirrhosis, which carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. For HCV, 15-45% of infected persons spontaneously clear the virus within six months; the remaining 55-85% progress to chronic infection, with a 15-30% risk of cirrhosis after 20 years. HCV can also cause extrahepatic manifestations such as depression, diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Target groups for screening
tables.caption: Target groups for screening
tables.content:
All persons in Eswatini should be offered HBV and HCV testing at least once; the following groups should be prioritised:
- Patients with clinical or laboratory suspicion of acute or chronic hepatitis
- All pregnant women (HBV as part of the HIV/syphilis/HBsAg triple test in antenatal care; HCV where risk factors are present)
- People living with HIV, and people with known HCV infection
- Household contacts and sexual partners of a person with HBV or HCV
- Children born to HBsAg-positive mothers
- Health workers and students in health-related training, and other frontline personnel (police, armed forces)
- Blood, tissue and organ donors and recipients; haemodialysis patients
- Prisoners and other closed settings
- Key populations: people who inject or use drugs, sex workers, men who have sex with men
- Adolescents and young people, and persons with multiple sexual partners
- People born before 2004 (before hepatitis B vaccine was introduced into the national schedule)

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Diagnosis of hepatitis B
tables.caption: Diagnosis of hepatitis B
tables.content:
Diagnosis is based on detection of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), using a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or ELISA on whole blood, capillary blood, dried blood spot, serum or plasma. A second positive HBsAg result after at least 6 months confirms chronic HBV infection. Where available, HBeAg and HBV DNA (viral load) further
stage the infection and inform treatment eligibility but are not required to diagnose chronic infection.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Diagnosis of hepatitis C
tables.caption: Diagnosis of hepatitis C
tables.content: Initial diagnosis is serological, using an RDT or ELISA for anti-HCV antibodies; a non-reactive result indicates no infection. A reactive antibody test indicates exposure only, and must be confirmed with a molecular test for HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) or HCV core antigen to distinguish current from past, spontaneously-cleared infection. If recent infection is suspected, a negative confirmatory test should be repeated 12-24 weeks later before infection is excluded.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Prevention
tables.caption: Prevention
tables.content: General prevention measures - infection prevention and control precautions, safe blood transfusion, injection and surgical safety, condom use, and hepatitis B vaccination of priority groups - are described in the STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention section (Section 3). There is currently no vaccine against hepatitis C. Sexual partners of a person with HBV should be tested and, if not immune, offered vaccine; sexual partners of a person with HCV should be tested with an anti-HCV test.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Prevention of hepatitis B mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)
tables.caption: Prevention of hepatitis B mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)
tables.content: Most chronic HBV infection is acquired perinatally or in early childhood, and infection acquired as a neonate becomes chronic in about 90% of cases, compared with under 5% when acquired as an adult. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis and HBsAg at least once, as early as possible in pregnancy, or at admission for delivery if not previously tested. Since 2020 WHO has recommended antiviral (tenofovir, TDF) prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA ( ≥ 200 000 IU/mL) or a positive HBeAg test, given from at least the second trimester until delivery. Where HBV DNA or HBeAg testing is not available, the 2024 WHO guideline recommends offering TDF prophylaxis to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women and adolescent girls. Regardless of maternal antiviral prophylaxis, every infant should receive a timely birth-dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by the remaining doses in the national EPI schedule; there is no evidence that caesarean delivery reduces HBV transmission risk, so standard obstetric practice should be followed.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Prevention of hepatitis B mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) > Figure 12
tables.caption: Figure 12: Algorithm on use of antiviral prophylaxis for prevention of mother-to-child transmission in pregnant women and adolescent girls with CHB, and assessment of treatment eligibility for their own health (WHO, 2024)
tables.content:
1 Serological testing: HBsAg testing in pregnant women and adolescent girls (using RDT or laboratory-based immunoassay) → HBsAg +ve / HBsAg -ve.
2 Assessment for antiviral prophylaxis (HBsAg +ve): assessment of eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis → HBV DNA or HBeAg testing available / not available.
3 Maternal intervention - antiviral prophylaxis:
- HBV DNA <200,000 IU/mL or HBeAg negative → no maternal tenofovir prophylaxis.
- HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL or HBeAg positive → start maternal tenofovir prophylaxis (from at least second trimester of pregnancy until at least after delivery).
- Testing not available → offer maternal tenofovir prophylaxis to all HBsAg +ve pregnant women and adolescents.
4 Maternal intervention - long-term antiviral treatment: assessment of eligibility for long-term treatment in pregnant women and adolescent girls for their own health: 1. significant fibrosis (≥F2) or cirrhosis (F4) regardless of HBV DNA or ALT levels (clinical criteria for cirrhosis; non-invasive tests: APRI >0.5 or transient elastography >7 kPa (adults)); OR 2. HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL AND ALT level > ULN; OR 3. presence of any of the following: coinfection (e.g. HIV, HDV, HCV); family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis; immune suppression; comorbidities (e.g. diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease); extrahepatic manifestations (e.g. glomerulonephritis or vasculitis); OR 4. persistently abnormal ALT levels alone (in absence of access to HBV DNA assay).
5 Infant interventions: hepatitis B birth dose vaccination of the infant followed by 2 or 3 doses of vaccine.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Newborn care and follow-up of infants exposed to HBV
tables.caption: Newborn care and follow-up of infants exposed to HBV
tables.content: All newborns should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth regardless of the mother's HBV status, with particular attention to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers; subsequent doses follow the national EPI schedule. If birth does not occur at a health facility, the birth dose should be given at first contact with a health facility. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in HBV infection. HBsAg testing of an exposed infant is unreliable before 6 months of age; exposed infants should be tested for HBsAg between 6 and 12 months, and referred for specialist evaluation if chronic infection (HBsAg positive for 6 months or more) is confirmed.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Prevention of hepatitis C vertical transmission
tables.caption: Prevention of hepatitis C vertical transmission
tables.content:
HCV vertical transmission occurs less often than with HBV (under 5-10% of pregnancies). There is currently no vaccine or antiviral prophylaxis to prevent HCV
vertical transmission, and DAA treatment is not recommended during pregnancy. There is no evidence to recommend a particular mode of delivery for this purpose, though prolonged rupture of membranes (over 6 hours) and invasive procedures during delivery should be avoided where possible; breastfeeding is not contraindicated. Maternal anti-HCV antibody can persist in an infant up to 18 months of age without indicating true infection; testing of an HCV-exposed child should therefore use anti-HCV serology after 18 months, confirmed by HCV RNA if positive. A child with a positive antibody test and detectable HCV RNA after 18 months has confirmed chronic HCV infection and should be referred to a paediatrician.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment of chronic hepatitis B
tables.caption: Treatment of chronic hepatitis B
tables.content: The goal of treatment is to prevent progression to cirrhosis, liver failure and hepatocellular carcinoma, and to improve survival; sustained suppression of HBV DNA is the primary marker of treatment success. Acute HBV infection does not usually require treatment, since most adults clear it spontaneously; antiviral treatment is occasionally needed for severe/fulminant acute hepatitis or in immunocompromised patients.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment eligibility
tables.caption: Treatment eligibility

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment regimen
tables.caption: Treatment regimen
tables.content:
For all adults, adolescents and children aged 2 years or older who need antiviral therapy, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV) - nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance - are the preferred first-line regimens, used as monotherapy rather than combined. Where TDF monotherapy is not available, TDF plus lamivudine (3TC) or TDF plus emtricitabine (FTC) is an acceptable alternative first-line regimen. Entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is
preferred for people with osteoporosis or impaired renal function. Older agents - telbivudine, lamivudine monotherapy and adefovir - are no longer recommended except on specialist advice, owing to a low barrier to resistance.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment of chronic hepatitis B > Treatment regimen > Figure 13
tables.caption: Figure 13: First-line antiviral regimens for chronic hepatitis B, by population (WHO, 2024)
tables.content:
Population | preferred first-line regimen | alternative first-line regimen | special circumstances:
- Adults: preferred TDF or ETV; alternative TDF + 3TC or TDF + FTC (where TDF monotherapy is not available); special circumstances: ETV or TAF (for people with established osteoporosis and/or impaired kidney function).
- Adolescents (12-17 years): preferred TDF or ETV; alternative TDF + 3TC, TDF + FTC (where TDF monotherapy is not available), TAF; special circumstances as for adults.
- Children (2-11 years): preferred TDF* or ETV.
TDF: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate; ETV: entecavir; 3TC: lamivudine; FTC: emtricitabine; TAF: tenofovir alafenamide fumarate. *Low dose formulations of TDF may not be widely available.

Caption note: adult doses: tenofovir 300 mg once daily (caution in renal impairment); entecavir 0.5 mg once daily (compensated liver disease, treatment-naïve) or 1 mg once daily (decompensated cirrhosis or prior lamivudine exposure). Paediatric entecavir is weight-banded from 0.15 mg (10-11 kg) to 0.5 mg (>30 kg); tenofovir 300 mg daily from age 12 and >35 kg.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment of chronic hepatitis B > Figure 14
tables.caption: Figure 14: Algorithm for assessment, treatment and monitoring of people with chronic hepatitis B infection (WHO, 2024)
tables.content:
HBsAg positive →
Initial assessment - assessment for treatment eligibility: 1. severity of liver disease using non-invasive tests (APRI or transient elastography); 2. ALT and HBV DNA level; 3. medical history: screening for presence of coinfections (e.g. HIV, HDV or HCV), comorbidities (e.g. diabetes, steatotic liver disease), immune suppression (e.g. long-term steroids, transplant), extrahepatic manifestations (e.g. glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), or family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis. General care measures: 1. counselling on lifestyle (e.g. alcohol consumption, diet and physical activity); 2. preparation for starting treatment (e.g. adherence support, risk factors for renal dysfunction and baseline renal function as indicated); 3. preventive measures (e.g. HBsAg screening of family and household members and sexual contacts, with HBV vaccination of those negative).
Treatment eligibility - treat all adults and adolescents (aged ≥12 years) (including pregnant and non-pregnant women and girls of reproductive age) with: 1. significant fibrosis (≥F2) or cirrhosis (F4) regardless of HBV DNA or ALT levels (clinical criteria for cirrhosis; non-invasive tests: APRI >0.5 or transient elastography >7 kPa (adults)); OR 2. HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL AND ALT level > ULN; OR 3. presence of any of the following (regardless of APRI score, HBV DNA or ALT level): coinfection (e.g. HIV, HDV, HCV); family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis; immune suppression; comorbidities (e.g. diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease); extrahepatic manifestations (e.g. glomerulonephritis or vasculitis); OR (in absence of access to HBV DNA assay) 4. persistently abnormal ALT levels alone.
Antiviral treatment regimen: initiate antiviral therapy and monitor: TDF or ETV; TDF + 3TC or TDF + FTC (if no access to TDF monotherapy); ETV or TAF in persons with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function or in children and adolescents.
Defer treatment and monitor if: ALT persistently normal AND HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL AND absence of coinfections, comorbidities, immune suppression, extrahepatic manifestations, family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis.
Monitoring: every 6 months - surveillance for HCC (AFP and ultrasound) (persons with cirrhosis or family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis); every 12 months - treatment response and/or disease progression: adherence at each visit, if on treatment; non-invasive tests (APRI or transient elastography); ALT and HBV DNA level; monitoring of renal function (creatinine), as indicated.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis B and C viral infection > Treatment monitoring
tables.caption: Treatment monitoring
tables.content: People on treatment should be monitored at least annually with a non-invasive test (APRI or transient elastography) for fibrosis/cirrhosis progression, ALT (and AST for APRI), and HBV DNA and HBeAg/anti-HBe where available; adherence should be assessed at every visit. More frequent monitoring, every 3-6 months, is recommended during the first year of treatment, for people with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, where adherence is a concern, for people with HIV coinfection, and for people with renal impairment. People with cirrhosis or a family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis should additionally be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma (ultrasound and AFP) every 6 months.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Viral Hepatitis and HIV Co-infection
tables.caption: Viral Hepatitis and HIV Co-infection
tables.content: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV co-infection with HIV is commonly found in HBV-endemic countries in Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and South America. HIV and HBV/ HCV share transmission routes; globally an estimated 2.73 million people are co-infected with HIV and HBV, and 2.3 million with HIV and HCV. As antiretroviral therapy (ART) has reduced HIV-associated opportunistic infections and mortality, HBV/HCV-related liver disease has become a leading cause of death among people living with HIV in some settings. Prevalence of HIV/HCV coinfection is generally higher where injection drug use is a primary route of HIV transmission. See Section 12.0 for guidance specific to HBV/HIV co-infected patients, including the choice of ART regimen.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Description and etiology
tables.caption: Description and etiology
tables.content: Hepatitis C is a bloodborne viral infection of the liver. Most infections occur through injection drug use, unsterile equipment used for tribal markings/scarification, unsafe injection or other healthcare practices, and use of unscreened blood for transfusion; sexual practices that expose a partner to blood can also transmit HCV.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Treatment of chronic hepatitis C
tables.caption: Treatment of chronic hepatitis C
tables.content: HCV infection is curable. WHO recommends pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens for all adults, adolescents and children aged 3 years and above with chronic HCV, regardless of disease stage, to prevent progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and to stop onward transmission. Pangenotypic regimens remove the need for genotyping before starting treatment. Fibrosis assessment (APRI or transient elastography) can help determine whether cirrhosis is present and the follow-up needed after cure, but should not delay treatment initiation. DAAs have very few contraindications with other medicines and few side-effects, so routine toxicity monitoring can be limited to a specimen at the start and end of treatment. The goals of treatment are to achieve a sustained virologic response (cure), prevent progression to complications, prevent onward transmission, and improve quality of life.

- Adults (18 years and above): 12 weeks | 12 weeks | 8 weeks | 12 weeks
- Adolescents (12-17 years): 12 | 12 | 8 | 12 weeks
- Older children (6-11 years): 12 | 12 | 8 | 12 weeks

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Assessment of treatment response and monitoring
tables.caption: Assessment of treatment response and monitoring
tables.content:
A single undetectable HCV RNA result 12 weeks after completing treatment (SVR12), by qualitative or quantitative NAT assay, is the benchmark for cure. Routine laboratory monitoring (full blood count, creatinine, AST/ALT) can be limited to a
baseline and end-of-treatment specimen. People with cirrhosis should have ultrasound and/or AFP for hepatocellular carcinoma every 6 months.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Management of treatment interruption
tables.caption: Management of treatment interruption
tables.content:
Treatment interruption (missing at least 7 consecutive days of DAA therapy) is more common in patients who are difficult to follow up, such as people experiencing homelessness or people who use drugs; missing a couple of doses usually does not affect treatment success. Management depends on how much treatment had been completed before the interruption:
- On treatment for under 4 weeks: assess the reason for interruption, provide counselling and, if the patient wishes to continue, restart the regimen from the beginning.
- On treatment for 4-8 weeks: extend the treatment duration by the length of the interruption.
- On treatment for over 8 weeks: if the interruption was under 2 weeks, extend treatment by the interruption length. If 2 weeks or more: for non-cirrhotic patients in areas with low genotype-3 prevalence, stop treatment and check HCV RNA 12 weeks later; for cirrhotic patients or areas with high genotype-3 prevalence, extend treatment to complete the full planned course and check HCV RNA 12 weeks after completion. Document the interruption, management plan and follow-up result clearly in the notes.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Treatment of chronic hepatitis C > Figure 17
tables.caption: Figure 17: Algorithm for screening, diagnosis, assessment, treatment and follow-up of people with chronic HCV infection (WHO)
tables.content:
1 Serological testing: conduct anti-HCV antibody testing (use rapid diagnostic test or laboratory-based immunoassay) → anti-HCV + / anti-HCV -.
2 Confirmation of current infection (anti-HCV +): proceed to viral load testing - use lab-based HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) or HCV core antigen (cAg) assays or point-of-care HCV RNA assays → HCV RNA test + or cAg+ = HCV viraemic infection; HCV RNA test - or cAg- = no HCV viraemic infection.
3 Treatment assessment: offer and start treatment for adults (≥18 years), adolescents (12-17 years) and children (≥3 years). Assess before treatment initiation: liver fibrosis with non-invasive testing (e.g. APRI, FIB-4) to determine if there is cirrhosis; other considerations (comorbidities, pregnancy, potential drug-drug interactions).
- ≥18 years and 3-17 years without cirrhosis: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 12 weeks; sofosbuvir/daclatasvir 12 weeks; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir 8 weeks.
- ≥18 years and 3-17 years with compensated cirrhosis: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 12 weeks; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir 8 weeks*; sofosbuvir/daclatasvir 24 weeks; sofosbuvir/daclatasvir 12 weeks**.
4 Monitoring: assess cure - sustained virological response (SVR) at 12 weeks after the end of treatment (HCV RNA SVR, qualitative or quantitative nucleic acid test [NAT]); detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in persons with cirrhosis (every 6 months) with ultrasound or AFP.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Special populations
tables.caption: Special populations
tables.content:
- Renal impairment: Daclatasvir, velpatasvir and voxilaprevir need no dose adjustment in renal failure; sofosbuvir, previously avoided when creatinine clearance was under 30 mL/min, is now considered safe even in end-stage renal failure. Ribavirin should be avoided when eGFR is under 30.
- HIV/HCV co-infection: liver disease progresses faster even when HIV is well controlled, so this group is prioritised for HCV treatment; whether to treat HCV before or alongside ART should be decided case-by-case, particularly because of drug-drug interactions.
- HBV/HCV co-infection: HCV is usually the main driver of liver inflammation, but HBV reactivation is possible during DAA treatment, particularly in patients with cirrhosis, where it can precipitate liver failure. Patients who meet HBV treatment criteria should start lifelong HBV treatment alongside HCV treatment; where lifelong HBV treatment is not available, HBV treatment should continue at least until HCV treatment is complete.
- People who use drugs: people who use drugs are at risk of re-infection if needle sharing continues; adequate needle and syringe programmes (NSP) and opioid substitution therapy (OST) reduce HCV incidence, and OST alone has been shown to reduce transmission by 50-80%. Treatment should not be withheld because of concerns about adherence or reinfection - treating this group reduces HCV prevalence and transmission, especially combined with NSP/OST and peer support. People who remain at risk after cure should be tested with HCV antibody every 12 months if antibody-negative, or with HCV RNA (not antibody, which can remain positive lifelong) if previously cured.

tables.heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI’s And Related Clinical Conditions > Hepatitis C (HCV) > Prevention
tables.caption: Prevention
tables.content: Sexual partners of a person with HCV should be screened with an anti-HCV test. As there is no vaccine against HCV, prevention relies on infection prevention and control measures, safe blood and injection practices, and harm-reduction services (needle and syringe programmes, opioid substitution therapy) for people who use drugs.

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men
tables.caption: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men
tables.content:
STI’s in men who have sex with men (MSM) are no different from STI’s in the rest of the population, but the types of sexual practices determine the site where STI’s occur. STI’s in MSM can be transmitted by penile-anal contact, oro-anal contact, or fingering. Ano-genital symptoms can result due to penile-anal contact. Symptoms due to peri-anal ulcers (for example, herpes, chancroid and syphilis) and warts can cause pain, tenesmus, bleeding, and discharge. Oro-anal intercourse can lead to the transmission of a wide variety of other organisms normally transmitted by the feaco-oral route.
These include hepatitis A virus, shigella, salmonella, and giardia, resulting in gastro-intestinal symptoms. Anal intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma may follow infection with high-risk subtypes of human papilloma virus. Oral and peri-oral symptoms can result because of oro-genital sexual activity. Oral STI’s usually are asymptomatic. Neisseria gonorrhoea and Chlamydia infect the pharyngeal mucosa readily, but rarely cause pharyngeal infections. Syphilis, chancroid and herpes may cause ulcers on the tongue, oral mucosa, palate or lips. Warts may develop in and around the mouth.

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Management of STI’s in men who have sex with men
tables.caption: Management of STI’s in men who have sex with men
tables.content:
In general, the clinical management of STI’s in MSM is the same as outlined elsewhere in this document earlier. The service provider should conduct rectal and
oro-pharyngeal examinations when providing care to MSM. Additional infections common in MSM that are not covered in the flow charts include oral or pharyngeal and ano-rectal STI’s, and are described below. Service providers should be aware that oral and anal STI’s can also occur in female patients practicing oral or anal sex. Therefore, as a standard of care every patient (irrespective of sex or gender) should be examined thoroughly to exclude STI’s in these sites.

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Management of sexually transmitted pharyngitis
tables.caption: Management of sexually transmitted pharyngitis
tables.content: Clinically, it is difficult to diagnose gonococcal or chlamydial pharyngitis reliably. Additionally, service providers should be aware that pharyngeal gonorrhoea can be more difficult to clear than urethral infections. Other oro-pharyngeal STI’s (such as herpes and warts) can often be detected by physical examination and can be managed according to the treatment guidelines. It is recommended that whenever a MSM patient is suffering from significant pharyngitis, and a history of unprotected oral sex makes pharyngeal gonococcal or chlamydial infection a likely risk, the patient should be treated syndromically

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Treatment for sexually-transmitted Pharyngitis
tables.caption: Treatment for sexually-transmitted Pharyngitis
tables.content:
- Ceftriaxone 1g STAT (to treat gonococcal infection) PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT (to treat chlamydial infection)

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Management of sexually transmitted ano-rectal infections or proctitis
tables.caption: Management of sexually transmitted ano-rectal infections or proctitis
tables.content:
Proctitis is an inflammation of the rectal wall and is the most common reaction to an ano-rectal STI (due to gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia or herpes). Anyone whose immune system is impaired is at increased risk of developing proctitis, particularly from infections caused by the herpes simplex virus or cytomegalovirus, or from reactivation of an earlier infection.
Proctitis may be caused by Salmonella spp, Shigella spp, or Entamoeba histolytica as a part of gastroenteritis, which may manifest as diarrhoea with fever, anorexia, and abdominal cramps. Antibiotics that destroy normal intestinal bacteria and allow
other bacteria to grow in their place may also cause proctitis. Herpes proctitis may be mistaken for the rectal manifestation of ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.
Proctitis typically causes painless bleeding or the passage of mucus (sometimes mistaken for diarrhoea) from the rectum. There may also be ineffectual straining to defecate (“tenesmus”), sometimes mistakenly described as “constipation” by patients. The anus and rectum may be intensely painful, with external and internal ulceration, when the cause is gonorrhoea, herpes, or cytomegalovirus infection. A proctoscopic examination (which should be done, if feasible) will reveal rectal pus, bleeding or ulceration.
All cases of proctitis in MSM should be treated for gonorrhoea and chlamydia infections. Symptoms of diarrhoea, bloody stools, abdominal cramping, nausea, and/or bloating may indicate giardia infection or amoebic dysentery. Most bacterial diarrheal diseases resolve spontaneously with oral rehydration and anti-diarrheal medication. Ano-rectal infections are a potent co-factor for HIV transmission. The service provider should counsel the patient on consistent and correct use of condoms during anal or oral sex to prevent STI’s and HIV infections.

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Treatment for sexually transmitted proctitis
tables.caption: Treatment for sexually transmitted proctitis
tables.content:
- Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM STAT (to treat gonococcal infection) PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT (to treat chlamydial infection) If symptoms of diarrhoea, bloody stools, abdominal cramping, nausea, and/or bloating are present: Add treatment for diarrhoea according to local epidemiology, including oral rehydration

tables.heading_path: 8.0 STI’S in Men Who Have Sex With Men > Flowchart for management of sexually transmitted ano-rectal infections or proctitis
tables.caption: Flowchart for management of sexually transmitted ano-rectal infections or proctitis
tables.content:
Pain and itchiness → Take history; examine patient including ano-genital area. Then:
- Ano-rectal ulcer present? YES → Benzathine Penicillin, 2.4 million units I.M stat PLUS Azithromycin, 1g, orally stat PLUS Acyclovir, 400mg orally TDS for 7 days. Health promotion package and follow up after 7 days → Follow-up at 7 days: ulcers and enlargement lymph nodes present? (NO → Reinforce health promotion. YES → Re-infected or poor compliance → Repeat treatment and re-inforce health promotion package.)
- Anal discharge present? YES → Ceftriaxone, 500 mg IM stat PLUS Doxycycline 100mg bd 14 day or Azithromycin 1gm stat → Follow-up at 7 days: improved? (YES → Reinforce health promotion. NO → Re-infected or poor compliance → Repeat treatment and re-inforce health promotion package.)

Health promotion package: educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment; promote abstinence or condom use during treatment; promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants; issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment; offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines; offer voluntary medical male circumcision; offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.

tables.heading_path: 9.0 STI’s In Mobile Populations
tables.caption: 9.0 STI’s In Mobile Populations
tables.content: SADC governments are concerned that the movement of people between Member States is a major factor in the spread of HIV and other STI’s. Today there is increasing recognition that mobile populations (including truck drivers or transport workers, migrant workers, domestic workers, farm workers, military personnel and refugees) are more vulnerable to STI’s and HIV than non-migrating populations. They may have little or no access to health information, health services and means of STI or HIV prevention (such as condoms) or treatment of STI’s. They may also be at higher risk due to additional factors such as discrimination, exploitation, harassment, and scant legal or social protection in the host community.

tables.caption: Management

tables.heading_path: 10.0 STI’s In Prisoners and Detainees
tables.caption: 10.0 STI’s In Prisoners and Detainees
tables.content:
Addressing STI’s as new detainees arrive can mitigate the possibility of transmission of STI’s within detention and prison facilities. In general, it is recommended that all new prisoners or detainees should have a thorough health assessment upon intake, and that identified STI’s should be treated immediately.
Additionally, the new detainees should be offered HIV counseling and testing; Condoms should be available in prisons and should be distributed among detainees to prevent infections. STI management and treatment in prisoners or detainees is the same as outlined in the previous sections.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents
tables.caption: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents
tables.content:
The occurrence of STI’s in children with the exception of neonatal infections and congenital syphilis invariably indicates sexual abuse. Health workers therefore should arrange for emotional as well as legal support for the child as part of the comprehensive management. In rare instances, however, chlamydial vaginitis acquired perinatally could manifest up to the age of three. Genital warts are not specific indicators of abuse unless supported by other evidence. Bacterial vaginitis has been diagnosed in children who have been abused, but its presence alone does not prove sexual abuse. Candidiasis is not a sexually transmitted infection in adults or children.
STI in adolescents place them at a higher risk of acquiring HIV. This is because the same biological and social factors that increase vulnerability to STI also increase vulnerability to HIV infection.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > Mucosal tear during sexual act
tables.caption: Mucosal tear during sexual act
tables.content: - Underdeveloped vaginal epithelium, leading to interruption in mucosal integrity which could be easily infected by aetiologies of STI and HIV.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > Social factors
tables.caption: Social factors
tables.content:
- Multiple sexual partnerships
- Commercial sex
- Poor health seeking behaviour
- Low self-esteem
- Lack of youth friendly services The following key issues are useful to remember during management of STI in adolescents
- Adolescents may have limited access to health care and may not seek care adequately. therefore, arrangements should be made to ensure compliance and future follow up.
- Partner notification and management is often difficult, thus risk of re-infection exists.
- Pregnancy should be considered and screening is pertinent in adolescent females.
Syndromes in children and adolescents are caused by similar pathogens as in adults and thus follow similar management principles. However, some medications used in adults may not be used for children. See Annex 5 and 5.1

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.1 Congenital syphilis
tables.caption: 11.1 Congenital syphilis
tables.content:
Congenital syphilis may occur if the pregnant mother has syphilis. However, the risk is minimal if she has been given penicillin during pregnancy.
- All infants of RPR/RDT-Tp/VDRL-reactive mothers should be examined at birth and at 3 months intervals until it is confirmed that serological tests are, and remain, negative. Any antibody carried over from mother to baby usually disappears within 3 months of birth.
- It is recommended that all infants born to RPR/RDT-Tp/VDRL- reactive mothers, should be treated with a single IM dose of Benzathine Penicillin, 50, 000 IU/kg, whether or not the mothers were treated during pregnancy (with or without penicillin).
- Hospitalization is recommended for all symptomatic babies born to mothers who were RPR/RDT-Tp/VDRL-reactive.
Congenital syphilis is divided into early (first 2 years of life) and late (becomes apparent later in life).
Signs and symptoms of early congenital syphilis More commonly, a child aged 2 to 12 weeks is brought in with a history of failure to thrive and having a generalised bullous or papulosquamous rash. The rash may cover the entire body but usually affects the buttocks, thighs, face, palms and soles. Occasionally, flat grey condylomata lata lesions may be seen in body folds. There may be generalised lymphadenopathy, enlargement of liver and spleen and anaemia. Since the infection is systemic, any organ of the body may be affected.
Diagnosis of latent (early or late) congenital syphilis the diagnosis of latent (early or late) congenital syphilis is usually made during routine testing of an asymptomatic child whose mother has a positive syphilis blood test. Such cases should be referred to a higher level for thorough examination, including cerebrospinal fluid examination to rule out latent neurosyphilis.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.1 Congenital syphilis > Management
tables.caption: Management
tables.content:
Recommended regimens for early congenital syphilis (up to 2 years of age) Symptomatic infants and asymptomatic infants (up to two years of age) should be treated for early congenital syphilis:
- Aqueous Penicillin, 100,000~150,000 IU/kg/day IV in 2 divided doses daily for 10 days administered as 50,000 IU/kg/dose IV every 12 hours, during the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter for a total of 10 days. OR
- Procaine Penicillin, 50,000 IU/kg IM in a single daily dose for 10 days.
Antimicrobials other than penicillin (such as Erythromycin) are not recommended for congenital syphilis, except in cases of allergy to penicillin. Tetracyclines should not be used in young children.
Recommended regimens for late congenital syphilis (more than 2 years duration)
- Aqueous Penicillin 200, 00 to 300,000 IU/kg/day IV or IM in divide doses (50,000IU/ kg/dose every 4-6 hours) for 10-14 days. For penicillin hypersensitive patients (after the first month of life):
- Erythromycin base / stearate, 7.5-12.5 mg/kg/day orally QID for 30 days.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.3 Neonatal Herpes
tables.caption: 11.3 Neonatal Herpes
tables.content: Neonatal herpes Neonatal herpes may occur after birth in a neonate whose mother had active herpes lesions in her genitalia during labour. Signs and symptoms may include severe mucosal or skin rash, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis and it is frequently fatal. Suspected neonatal herpes case should be referred immediately to the higher level. Caesarean section for a pregnant mother having genital herpes lesions during the third trimester of pregnancy or at the time labour should be advised as a preventive measure.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.4 Neonatal conjunctivitis
tables.caption: 11.4 Neonatal conjunctivitis
tables.content: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) presenting in a child beyond the immediate neonatal period is managed as described in section 4.7. As with all cases identified after the neonatal window, sexual abuse must be excluded (see section 11.5).

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.5 Management of STI’s in very young children (beyond neonatal period and up to 10 years of age)
tables.caption: 11.5 Management of STI’s in very young children (beyond neonatal period and up to 10 years of age)
tables.content:
The identification of a sexually transmissible agent in a child beyond the neonatal period, in the vast majority of cases, is suggestive of sexual abuse. However, exceptions do exist: for example, rectal or genital infection with C. trachomatis in very young children may be caused by peri-natally acquired infection, which may persist for up to 3 years. In addition, bacterial vaginosis and genital warts have been identified in both abused and non-abused children.
- When the only evidence of abuse is the isolation of an organism or the detection of antibodies to a sexually transmissible agent, findings should be carefully confirmed and considered.
- Service providers who suspect abuse must consider referral to specialized counselling, psychological and social support services for the complete management of these patients.
- STI prophylaxis or presumptive treatment for gonorrhea and chlamydia in a sexually abused child is not recommended, since very young girls appear to be at lower risk of ascending infection than adolescents or adult women. However, in light of increased risk for HIV transmission, these children should be referred to the higher level for child-centred psychological counselling, as well as for further clinical management.
- STI’s in pre-adolescents and adolescents (children 10 years and older) There are differences in the epidemiology of STI’s in adolescents and adults, because adolescents are regarded as being more biologically susceptible to infection and at increased risk of morbidity. However, in the majority of cases, the presentation of STI’s is similar to that seen in adults. The most important differences are as follows:
- At the time of puberty and adolescence, the female genital tract undergoes changes in response to increasing levels of ovarian hormones.
- Along with anatomical and physiological changes, the vaginal epithelium begins to secrete mucus. The mucus secretion causes the adolescent girl to develop a white vaginal discharge, which is physiological. Generally, therefore, vaginal discharge is a poor predictor of the presence of either gonococcal or chlamydial infection.
- In pre-pubescent girls, the columnar epithelium of the endo-cervical canal extends to the vaginal portion of the cervix. This cervical ectropion, which is normally present in 60-80% of sexually active adolescents, is associated with an increased risk of C. trachomatis infection and N. gonorrhoea. Exposure to oncogenic high- risk types of human papilloma virus enhances the risk of dysplasia and carcinoma at an early age.
- Additionally, because cervical mucus production and humoral immunity are absent until ovulation begins, the risk of PID or cervical infections is higher in the sexually active adolescent exposed to infection as opposed to the adult woman.

tables.heading_path: 11.0 STI’s In Children and Adolescents > 11.6 Management of STI’s in pre-adolescents and adolescents (children 10 years and older)
tables.caption: 11.6 Management of STI’s in pre-adolescents and adolescents (children 10 years and older)
tables.content:
The management of STI’s in pre-adolescents and adolescents is similar to that of adults. Lower abdominal pain or pelvic inflammatory disease in pre-adolescents and adolescents approximately 85% of gonococcal infection in females will be
asymptomatic. However, there may be vulval itching, minor discharge, urethritis or proctitis. In pre-pubescent girls, a purulent vulvo-vaginitis may occur. Similarly, C. trachomatis infection is asymptomatic in the majority of cases. Symptoms that may occur are inter-menstrual bleeding, post-coital bleeding and an increase in vaginal secretions.
Vaginal discharge syndrome in pre-adolescents and adolescents C. albicans is uncommon in adolescents prior to puberty. If present, the adolescent may have a discharge, vulval itching, dyspareunia (painful intercourse), a peri-anal soreness or a fissuring at the introitus. Attacks of candida vulvitis may be cyclical in nature and correspond to menstruation.B Vaginitis does not produce a vulvitis, and the adolescent will not complain of itching or soreness.
Genital ulcer syndrome in pre-adolescents and adolescents Presentation of GUS is the same in adolescents and adults. The stages of syphilis and serological responses are the same as in adults. Genital warts in pre-adolescents and adolescents Warts present as condylomatous, papular or flat lesions, much the same as in adults. In most children, warts disappear spontaneously over months to three (3) years.
Other considerations in pre-adolescents and adolescents. Adolescents often lack information about existing services, such as where they are, what times they operate, how much they cost, etc. Even if they know about these services they are often reluctant to seek help for diagnosis and treatment. They are often embarrassed and worried about social stigmatization. They also fear negative reactions from service providers and are concerned about a lack of confidentiality.
Initiatives to make health services more adolescent-friendly and more responsive to their particular need should be considered; Service providers dealing with children and adolescents must show respect and maintain confidentiality

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV
tables.caption: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV
tables.content:
A strong relationship exists between STI’s and HIV infection.
- STI’s and HIV infection are associated with the same risk behaviors:
unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. Therefore, the same measures that prevent STI’s also prevent sexual transmission of HIV infection;
- The presence of STI’s has been found to facilitate the acquisition and transmission of HIV infection. Diseases that cause genital ulcers (such as syphilis, chancroid and genital herpes) can increase the risk of HIV transmission by up to 10-fold, and diseases causing discharge (especially gonorrhoea, chlamydial infection and trichomoniasis) can increase that risk by up to four-fold. Thus, early diagnosis and effective treatment of STI’s can contribute significantly towards the reduction in HIV transmission; and
- There is mounting evidence that some STI pathogens are more virulent in the presence of HIV related immune-deficiency. This might have consequences for treatment recommendations for STI’s, although more studies need to be carried out before changes can be proposed.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Management of STI’s in people living with HIV
tables.caption: Management of STI’s in people living with HIV
tables.content:
The following are requirements in suspected or confirmed HIV and STI co-infection in patients:
- HIV counseling and testing should be offered routinely for all STI’s patients. HIV testing may be considered as a priority in patients with severe or treatment-failure cases of STI’s, and should be done only after obtaining their consent, with proper pre-and post-test counselling and whilst ensuring confidentiality.
- The treatment regimens for various STI’s are the same in STI-HIV co-infected cases, as well as for non HIV/STI cases.
- In some cases of STI’s in the presence of HIV infection, larger doses and longer treatment duration of the drugs listed under the various STI syndromes and conditions may be required. Those patients should be followed up regularly for longer duration.
- Excessive use of anti-microbials should be avoided, since this is likely to lead to more rapid development of antibiotic resistance. Therefore, clinical judgment on proper and early referral is required.
- Although counseling of individual patients on risk reduction and prevention of transmission to partners should be done with all STI’s patients, this is of vital importance for those infected with HIV.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Genital ulcer syndrome
tables.caption: Genital ulcer syndrome
tables.content:
Genital ulcer syndrome and HIV infection Patients with GUS should be encouraged to be tested for HIV infection because of the frequent association of the two diseases, and the implications for clinical assessment and management.
- Treatment for GUS in HIV infected patients is the same as for non-HIV patients. However, careful follow-up is necessary to ensure adequacy of treatment. These patients are more likely to experience extensive and more severe forms of ulcerations, treatment failure and ulcers heal more slowly. Increased dose and a more prolonged duration of therapy might be necessary.
- Patients should followed up weekly until there is complete clearance of lesions.
- Patients should be counseled that GUS facilitates the transmission of HIV.
- Because data are limited concerning the therapeutic efficacy of Ceftriaxone and Azithromycin in chancroid, some specialists suggest using Erythromycin 500 mg orally QID for 7 day regimen for treating chancroid ulcers in HIV-infected persons;
- In HIV patients with Donovanosis, Gentamicin, 1mg/kg intravenous (IV) TDS should be added if improvement is not evident within the first few days of therapy.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Herpes and HIV infection
tables.caption: Herpes and HIV infection

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Urethral discharge syndrome and HIV infection
tables.caption: Urethral discharge syndrome and HIV infection
tables.content: Urethral discharge syndrome and HIV infection gonococcal, chlamydial and other non-gonococcal urethritis may facilitate HIV transmission, and patients should be made aware of this fact during counselling. Treatment is same as in a non-HIV patient.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Candidiasis and HIV infection
tables.caption: Candidiasis and HIV infection
tables.content:
Candidiasis and HIV infection Candidiasis affecting multiple sites, including oral cavity, vulva and vagina, glans, and prepuce often occurs in HIV disease. Relapses of candidiasis are frequent. Prolonged treatment and suppressive therapy with imidazoles is often required.
- Fluconazole, 150 mg orally as a single dose weekly for 6 months OR
- Clotrimazole, 500mg intra-vaginally weekly for 6 months.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Genital warts and HIV infection
tables.caption: Genital warts and HIV infection
tables.content: Genital warts and HIV infection there is high prevalence of genital warts in persons with HIV. The warts may be multifocal, extensive and poorly responsive to treatment, and there is a greater likelihood of malignant transformation.

tables.heading_path: 12.0 STI’S In People Living With HIV > Hepatitis B and HIV Co-infection
tables.caption: Hepatitis B and HIV Co-infection
tables.content: For the definition, clinical features, screening priorities and treatment of hepatitis B, see section 7.0 (Hepatitis B and C viral infection). In people living with HIV who are co-infected with hepatitis B virus, WHO recommends that the antiretroviral regimen include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), which is active against both viruses; TDF should not be discontinued or substituted without first reviewing HBV status, since stopping TDF in a person with HBV/HIV co-infection can precipitate a hepatitis flare. All patients co-infected with HBV and HIV should start antiviral treatment regardless of CD4 count, WHO clinical stage, or HBV/HIV viral load.

tables.heading_path: 13.0 Behaviour Change Communication for STI’s Management
tables.caption: 13.0 Behaviour Change Communication for STI’s Management

tables.heading_path: 13.0 Behaviour Change Communication for STI’s Management > 13.1 Behavior change messages
tables.caption: 13.1 Behavior change messages
tables.content:
Behavior change messages are similar to those for HIV, but should emphasize information about the complications and treatment of STI’s. Upgrading service providers’ knowledge and communication skills is usually a prerequisite to successful BCC interventions.
In order for the behavior change communication to be effective, there should be emphasis on:
- Increased knowledge: Behavior change communication should ensure that people have the basic facts about STI’s in a language, visual medium or other media that they can understand and relate to. Effectiveness will motivate the target group to change their behaviors in positive ways.
- Promotion of services for prevention and treatment: Health-seeking behavior should be a priority in all behavior change communication activities so that the individuals go for preventive health checkups, early treatment and regular follow-ups. The health facility should collaborate with private practitioners, informal health sector such as traditional health practitioners, as they may be the preferred health providers for many STI patients, by establishing referral linkages or providing necessary trainings to them to ensure quality patient management.
- Stimulation of community dialogue: Facility staff should collaborate with groupings such as NGOs, CBOs, faith-based organizations and workplaces in the catchment area to enhance the promotion of healthy sexual behavior, early health-seeking behavior and improve outcome of partner notification and tracing. There should be encouragement of group and focused group discussions about the underlying factors, such as risk behaviors, risk settings and the environments that increase risk for STI’s. Community dialogue will create a demand for information and services.
- Promotion of advocacy: Through advocacy, behavior change communication can ensure that policy makers and opinion leaders understand the necessity for STI interventions and approach them seriously.
- Advocacy should take place at all levels, from the primary to the tertiary level. Behavior change massages should be communicated to all, especially to the following high risk groups;
- MSM,
- Sex workers
- Adolescents and young people
- People who inject drugs(PWID)
- Migrants
- Substance abusers
- Multiple sexual partners

tables.heading_path: 13.0 Behaviour Change Communication for STI’s Management > 13.1 Behavior change messages > Community level
tables.caption: Community level
tables.content:
The health facility should sensitize and receive support on STI’s and HIV AND AIDS issues from community health committees, civil society organizations, schools, workplaces and political leaders in the catchment area. Managers of cross-border province or district health facilities should promote communication and sharing of surveillance information and management protocols for strengthening inter-country collaboration.
- Reduction of stigma and discrimination: Communication on STI’s should address stigma and discrimination and attempt to influence social responses from local government and policy makers.
- Facility staff should collaborate with social welfare departments (for example, to gain social assistance) and with other health- related public sectors, as appropriate.

tables.caption: Definition:

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.1 Facility-level quality assurance standards > Clinic structure
tables.caption: Clinic structure
tables.content:
- The internal structure of the clinic should, at a minimum, include the following to ensure physical privacy, auditory privacy and confidentiality of patient interviews and information.
- In the consultation room, the examination table should be positioned to provide adequate space at the end of the table to appropriately view the genitalia during speculum examination. An examination light should always be available for use in the consulting room
- In areas where a separate counseling room is not available, counseling should be provided in the consultation room.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.1 Facility-level quality assurance standards > Staff training and skills
tables.caption: Staff training and skills

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.1 Facility-level quality assurance standards > Ethical standards:
tables.caption: Ethical standards:

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.1 Facility-level quality assurance standards > Standard treatment guidelines
tables.caption: Standard treatment guidelines
tables.content:
- It is essential that the STI treatment recommendations should be standardized and that staff comply with STI clinical management guidelines.
- The treatment recommendations should be adapted, based on the local epidemiological and antimicrobial sensitivity information.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.1 Facility-level quality assurance standards > Allergic reactions management
tables.caption: Allergic reactions management
tables.content: - All clinics that administer antibiotic medications (particularly via intramuscular or intravenous injections) should be adequately equipped with emergency resuscitation drugs and equipment’s, and should be prepared for emergency management of an allergic or anaphylactic reaction.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral
tables.caption: 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral
tables.content: STI clinical quality assurance is a way of monitoring and evaluating the quality of STI services that are provided at health facilities to ensure that the services are in accordance with established guidelines, policies, norms and standards.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Service availability
tables.caption: Service availability
tables.content: In order to make health facilities more accessible and increase attendance by the target population, they should be open during times when the target population can conveniently access the services.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Staff training and skills
tables.caption: Staff training and skills
tables.content: All staff should have appropriate qualifications and training to perform their assigned tasks. Service providers should be able to perform all the basic clinical procedures (including speculum and bimanual examinations) that are necessary to diagnose and manage STI patients.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Standard treatment guidelines:
tables.caption: Standard treatment guidelines:
tables.content:
- Flow charts that describe the standardized approach should be readily available for the clinic staff and should be on display in each room where treatments are prescribed to patients;
- Each clinic should also ensure that all essential patient management medicines, equipment’s and consumables are adequate in quantity based on the patient load and maintained in good working order.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Referral network establishment
tables.caption: Referral network establishment

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Monitoring and evaluation
tables.caption: Monitoring and evaluation
tables.content:
Monitoring is the regular, methodical process of collecting data to determine the progress and achievements of a programme. The type of information collected may vary, but it is important that only the data required to obtain information that is needed for improving the overall quality of STI services should be collected. Specific monitoring parameters that can be collected fall into four (4) main categories:
- Service delivery; i.e documentation and reporting
- Staff performance;
- Client satisfaction and response;
- Resource needs and allocation.
- Indicator matrix for STI monitoring and evaluation core indicators.
- STI Framework monitoring and evaluation logic model Evaluation involves analysing and assessing a programme, or part of a programme, to determine its quality and progress toward achieving its goals and objectives. Evaluations helps self-evaluate and subsequently improve own practices and the overall programme. Periodic quality-of-care audits and assessments of drug and supply management are examples of programme evaluation.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Operations research
tables.caption: Operations research
tables.content: For more effective STI programming, data are needed to determine whether the STI case management services offered at the facility are effective in reducing STI prevalence among people using the services and whether STI patterns have changed in response to the intervention. The data collected may be related to clinical diagnosis, treatment, laboratory and behavioural characteristics that can be collected at periodic intervals from a cohort or a sample of persons attending STI clinics. That is, such studies could help to determine whether preventive and curative services have any effect on the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections syndromes and other STI conditions among facility attendees.

tables.heading_path: 14.0 Quality Assurance: > 14.2 Programme-level quality assurance, monitoring and referral > Management of STI medications and commodities
tables.caption: Management of STI medications and commodities
tables.content:
The trust in STI management gained through proper clinical examination and patient counselling could be severely eroded when STI drugs or condoms are out of stock or equipments malfunction when the patient uses the health facility.
- By all means avoid shortages of drugs, equipments, test kits and other essential commodities.
- Ensure proper management of asymptomatic and symptomatic STI cases in the community.
- Patients sometimes consult informal practitioners who cannot assure the quality of care. It is therefore imperative to strengthen STI drug and commodity management systems at health facilities.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance
tables.caption: 15.0 STI Surveillance
tables.content:
STI’s surveillance is an epidemiological exercise by which the spread of STI’s are monitored in order to establish patterns of progression. The main functions of STI surveillance is to record, observe, analyze, predict and understand STI trends to reduce the harm caused by STI’s, and to increase the knowledge about the factors that contribute to such trends. It is an essential component for the STI and HIV prevention programs. Accurate data enable strategic planning and provide information for advocacy, programme design, prioritization of interventions, monitoring and evaluation, and to improve the quality of patient care and overall programme effectiveness.
The following section provides practical guidance for strengthening the STI surveillance system to obtain meaningful data on STI’s that can directly facilitate effective planning, execution and monitoring of STI control and prevention efforts at all facility levels. This section also describes common core surveillance indicators that can provide a countries picture that is needed for the periodic review of policies, guidelines and protocols on STI-related issues in Eswatini.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.1 Prevalence assessment and monitoring:
tables.caption: 15.1 Prevalence assessment and monitoring:
tables.content:
The primary purposes of STI prevalence assessment and monitoring are to identify population subgroups with high prevalence of Sexually Transmitted Infections, and to
monitor trends in STI prevalence among defined populations (for example, women who are routinely screened for syphilis during antenatal care).
Prevalence data are of great use in STI programme planning, management and evaluation because they can be used to:
- Identify subgroups that are at high risk for HIV infection (as evidenced by high rates of Sexually Transmitted Infections);
- Guide funding and resource allocation for STI and HIV prevention programmes;
- Monitor the effectiveness of STI and HIV prevention programmes; and
- Develop national estimates of Sexually Transmitted Infections.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system:
tables.caption: 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system:
tables.content:
The core components of a good STI surveillance system that provides the necessary information for effective control programs are:
Case reporting is the process whereby service providers or laboratories report cases of disease to public health authorities.
- STI’s may be reported syndromically or etiologically, depending on the availability of laboratory tests in clinical care settings.
- Sentinel surveillance usually involves a select few healthcare facilities. A national control programme, preferably with the assistance of an epidemiologist and bio-statistician, should decide on the number of facilities to be involved in the STI surveillance. This will determine the number and level of service providers to be selected and trained.
The state of the HIV epidemic in Eswatini also has implications for activities and priorities for surveillance of Sexually Transmitted Infections.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system: > Case reporting has several purposes:
tables.caption: Case reporting has several purposes:

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system: > Prevalence assessment and monitoring
tables.caption: Prevalence assessment and monitoring
tables.content:
The primary purposes of STI prevalence assessment and monitoring are to identify population subgroups with high prevalence of Sexually Transmitted Infections, and to monitor trends in STI prevalence among defined populations. Prevalence data are of great use in STI programme planning, management and evaluation because they can be used to:
- Identify subgroups that are at high risk for HIV infection (as evidenced by high rates of Sexually Transmitted Infections)
- Guide funding and resource allocation for STI and HIV prevention programmes;
- Monitor the effectiveness of STI and HIV prevention programmes; and
- Develop national estimates of Sexually Transmitted Infections.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system: > Assessment of aetiology of infection
tables.caption: Assessment of aetiology of infection
tables.content: Periodic assessment of aetiologies of STI syndromes (such as urethral discharge, genital ulcer disease or vaginal discharge) provide data for guiding STI syndromic management, assist in the interpretation of syndromic case reports, and aid the assessment of disease burden due to specific pathogens. These data also may be used to evaluate syndromic management algorithms.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system: > Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Surveillance and Gonococcal Antibiogram Development
tables.caption: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Surveillance and Gonococcal Antibiogram Development
tables.content:
The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, both globally and within the SADC region, underscores the need for routine AMR surveillance as a core element of the national STI surveillance system. The primary objective of AMR surveillance is to generate high-quality data on antimicrobial susceptibility patterns to support the continuous revision of treatment protocols, optimize empiric treatment regimens, and identify emerging resistance mechanisms. A core element of this surveillance is to promote the use of available bacteriaology testing services for evidence generation and development of a
gonococcal antibiogram that will support the empiric tratement and for monitoring the resistance trends to guide the review of treatment strategies accordingly.

tables.heading_path: 15.0 STI Surveillance > 15.2 Core components of STI surveillance system: > Special studies
tables.caption: Special studies
tables.content:
Periodically, STI programmes shall perform special studies to address important STI surveillance issues that are not part of routine case reporting or prevalence assessments. Examples may include assessments of quality of care using mystery clients, or measuring incidence and prevalence of STI-related complications such as PID or ectopic pregnancy.
These studies can include estimation of the burden attributable to asymptomatic STI’s, investigations for outbreaks of particular infections, such as syphilis in certain populations and geographical settings.

tables.heading_path: Annexes > Annex 5: Precautions with penicillin administration
tables.caption: Annex 5: Precautions with penicillin administration
tables.content:
Precautions with penicillin administration
The recommended and most effective treatment for syphilis is Benzathine Penicillin; all patients who present with genital ulcer syndrome and/or positive syphilis serology should be treated with penicillin, unless it is clear that the patient is allergic to the drug. Before treating a patient with penicillin, clinic staff must ask the patient whether he or she has a history of allergic reaction to penicillin. If the patient answers “yes,” staff should explore the issue by asking the following questions:
- What was the patient’s age the time of the reaction?
- What were the characteristics of the reaction?
- How long after beginning penicillin therapy did the reaction begin?
- How was the penicillin administered?
- What other medications was the patient taking and at what time?
- What happened when the penicillin was discontinued?
- Has the patient taken any antibiotics similar to penicillin (Amoxicillin, Ampicillin or Cephalosporins) and, if so, what were the reactions?
The patient can be said to have a strong history of penicillin allergy when he or she reports reactions such as anaphylaxis, angioedema/urticaria, pruritic rash and bronchospasm. Symptoms such as maculo-papular rash, gastrointestinal upset or other unknown reactions are less predictive of an allergy. If the history of penicillin hypersensitivity is unknown or not elicited, administer an intradermal injection of 0.03ml of penicillin (test dose) on the left forearm of the patient. Observe the patient for 30 minutes. The appearance of wheals and redness indicates a positive sensitivity test. Staff should be prepared to manage anaphylactic reaction even with the test dose.
source_flags: Annex 5 advises an intradermal penicillin test dose when the allergy history is unknown; intradermal testing with undiluted penicillin is not a validated allergy test and can itself cause anaphylaxis (WHO and national programmes advise giving benzathine penicillin with anaphylaxis preparedness rather than routine skin testing).

tables.heading_path: Annexes > Annex 7. Behavioural change in STI
tables.caption: Annex 7. Behavioural change in STI
tables.content:
STI prevention is very crucial; clients must be encouraged to report any unprotected sexual encounter to the nearest health facility within 72 hours to allow effective management and integration of services, this can give opportunity to reduce unintended pregnancies as the clients can also be given PEP, emergency contraception (ECs).
Sexual encounters can be consented and not. In Eswatini there is currently high prevalence of SGBV which exposes clients to STIs,including HIV, as well as Hepatitis. There are groups which are considered high risk in contracting STIs and these include, AGYW, LGBTIQs, MSM, MCPs, PWIDs, FSW. Mentally challenged and People living with disability
Staff should explore the issue by asking the following questions:
- When was the last time you had an unprotected sexual encounter?
- If condom not used, Why
- Was it a consented sexual encounter? If no why…………….
- What information do you have about STIs?
- Do you have any unusual symptoms in your genital area?
- Have you ever been treated for STIs?
- Did you take and finish your medication?

## 7.1.2 Syphilis in pregnancy

The clinical symptoms of syphilis are not altered by pregnancy. Since asymptomatic adult syphilis infection is common, all pregnant women should be screened for syphilis. This can reduce the complications of congenital syphilis. A rapid plasma reagent (RPR) test should be routinely done on pregnant mothers at first contact with the health care provider and treatment should be instituted if the RPR result is reactive and the partner should be treated as well. If RPR test is negative repeat after 3 months.
